en: In the *Viśālāmalavatī*, a commentary on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, Chapter 2, it was stated that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Among these, perception has been explained.
Now, as the opportunity has arrived, he speaks in order to explain inference, beginning with the words "inference is twofold," and so forth.
That by which one realizes for oneself one's own welfare,
and that by which one causes others to realize theirs.
Now, it might be argued that the definition of the "for-the-sake-of-others" (parārtha) [inference] need not be stated separately.

For, by the very formulation of the definition of the "means of making known" (gamaka), the sequential order of the speaker's words has already been demonstrated; otherwise, if it were stated differently, it would fail to illuminate the properties of the means of making known.
Indeed, those who know a particular object in a certain way and are skilled in speech do not require further instruction when they proceed to communicate that object.
This is true;
nevertheless, this undertaking is for the purpose of instructing the ignorant.

For we observe that even when things are being explained exactly as they are, people speak otherwise; thus, there is the non-statement of the useful *avinābhāva* (invariable concomitance), and the employment of the useless *upanaya* (application) and *nigamana* (conclusion).
He went.
The ablative case in *trirūpāt* (from the three-featured) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in the expression "sound [arises] from impact.
Alternatively, it is used with the elision of a gerund suffix (*lyap-lope*), as in "having climbed the palace, he looks out" expressed as "he looks out from the palace.
Likewise, having seen the three-featured mark, there is the seeing of the object; thus, "the perception of the object from the three-featured mark."
(1) But is not the mention of the "three characteristics" (trirūpa) useless? For that which lacks the three characteristics cannot be a logical mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, a logical mark (liṅga) is so called because by means of it an "inferred object" (liṅgin)—that which is hidden—is made known;
and this is not possible without the possession of the three characteristics.
For this reason as well, since the meaning has already been conveyed, one should not say "from that which possesses the three characteristics."
This is not a fault;
for some maintain that a logical mark (liṅga) may possess even fewer than three forms.
Therefore, the mention of "three forms" is intended to eliminate such conflicting views.
In this regard, the shameless one (Ahrīka) says: "That which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*).
That object has but a single characteristic; it does not have four characteristics."
"Otherwise" means "without the probandum. "Inexplicability" (anupapannatva) means non-occurrence or impossibility.
But would this not simply be the state of being inseparable (avinābhāvitva)?
"No," says the shameless one.

For "inseparability" (avinābhāvitva) is intended to exist outside the probandum (*sādhya*), whereas "the impossibility of being otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*) exists only in the subject (*dharmin*) with respect to the probandum itself.
He states a verse as well: "The status of a logical reason (*hetu*) is accepted for that which is not seen apart from the probandum in the example."
Furthermore, for me, it is impossible for others to establish [the property] in the subject without this [reason].
(2) Thus [it is said].
And this is indeed a single characteristic.
Alternatively, if there were three characteristics, then "the impossibility of being otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*) must be accepted as a fourth characteristic.

For if it were merely the possession of the three characteristics [of a valid reason], then even the argument "he who has gone to another country is dark-skinned because he is the son of Caitra" would constitute a valid reason.
In this regard, as for what was stated—that "invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) is held by opponents to exist outside of the probandum (*sādhya*)"—this is a mere superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

For invariable concomitance is this pervasion (*vyāpti*), established through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*): "wherever there is the property that serves as the means of proof (*sādhanadharma*), there is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
Therefore, that [concomitance] is indeed accepted even with respect to the probandum itself.

Furthermore, if it were maintained that only that which is inseparably connected with the property to be proven (sādhya) within the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) alone is accepted as a logical reason (hetu), then in that case, that which possesses an inseparable connection with the property to be proven even outside [the subject] would not be a reason.
Moreover, even a deviant factor (vyabhicārin) would become a reason, since the condition of being "otherwise impossible" (anyathānupapannatva) could exist for it within the subject as well.
Therefore, this [position] is untenable.
Therefore, because this is illogical, a reason characterized by the four marks is not tenable.

Furthermore, as for what was stated— that if it were merely the possession of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*), then even "because he is the son of Caitra" would constitute a valid reason— that is incorrect.
For the three characteristics are established only for specific types of reasons— namely, essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)— and not for others.
And this [entity] is not included among them;
therefore, whence could that undesirable consequence arise?

But showing that the reason is of two kinds, he says: "Where a property of the subject, though unknown, is known and made known as being indeed present in the subject, this is a reason characterized by affirmation and negation."
Thus:
where a property (dharma) such as impermanence, which was previously unknown and sought after, is known in relation to a subject (dharmin) such as sound, based on a property such as being produced;
"knownness" is understood here by implication.

"Existing indeed"—this means that in the case of jars and other such things, it is either remembered by the cognizer himself or is made to be remembered by another in the context of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
That which possesses both affirmation and negation—namely, "existing indeed" and "not non-existing"—is the reason (*hetu*) characterized by affirmation and negation.

By this, the two-fold nature [of the reason] has been stated: namely, its being a property of the subject (*dharmidharmatva*) and its being a property of the existent probandum (*satsādhyadharmatva*).

In this context, by stating that the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) exists only where [the reason] is present and does not exist where it is absent, it is precisely the possession of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that has been expressed; for it is only when the reason is necessarily absent in the absence of that [property] that it exists only there [where the property is]. Therefore, the three-fold nature (trairūpya) has merely been stated in another form, and thus the reason is not two-fold.
(4) Another [scholar] maintains that the probans (*hetu*) has six characteristics.

These three—namely, having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), having the intended singular number (*viva-kṣitaikasaṅkhyatva*), and being known (*jñātatva*)—are [included therein]. Among these, first of all, "having an uncontradicted object" is not a distinct characteristic, because there is a contradiction between contradiction (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
For the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of a reason consists in its presence only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is present.
And how could that reason, characterized by such a definition, exist in the subject (*dharmin*) while the property to be proven is not there?
Therefore, there is no coexistence of sublation (*bādhā*) and inseparable connection.
Therefore, "having an uncontradicted object" is not a distinct characteristic.
Since there is no object to be excluded, the intended singularity of number should not be stated as a separate defining characteristic.
It is stated, however, for the purpose of avoiding the contingency that a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) might function as a valid reason (*hetu*).

Indeed, when two reasons possessing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and logical methods (*yukti*) are encountered together in a single instance as contradictories, the state of being a "non-deviant contradictory" arises.
Furthermore, no contradictory cause is possible for the effect, essential nature, and non-perception reasons as they have been defined.

For how could it be that one [reason] is non-deviant because it exists only when its own probandum exists, while another [reason] is contradictory because it exists only when that very same probandum is absent?
Moreover, if that reason exists by its very nature as possessing that property, then even upon the occurrence of some other factor, how could it ever become otherwise?
For it is impossible for things to undergo a change in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor is it possible for two contradictory natures to coexist.
If, on the other hand, [a reason] by its very nature does not possess that property, then even at another time it would not be a means of proof for anything.

Therefore, since a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) possessing those same characteristics cannot exist for a reason that, by its very nature, is inseparably connected with its own probandum and possesses the aforementioned definition, the desire to express a single number [as a characteristic] is itself without definition.

If it is argued that this entails the undesirable consequence of stating a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), there is no fault, because we accept a logical mark (*liṅga*) that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala*).
Furthermore, its specific object will be explained later.
Furthermore, knowledge is not a property of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
How then could there be a definition of the logical mark?

When considering what kind of form the logical mark must have for the object to be understood from it, the form of that which is non-deceptive for the cognizer is stated; by seeing which, one discriminates between the valid and invalid means of proof, and thereby gains conviction regarding the means of achieving the desired object.
It proceeds as follows:

therein, that which is the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of this mark (*liṅga*) is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), not its extrinsic form (*pararūpa*). This is because [the latter] would be over-extensive (*atiprasaṅga*) if mere utility in producing a cognition were sufficient for it to be a definition.
For if that were the case, even objects of cognition (*prameya*) such as the *puruṣa* (the primal person) and so forth would possess the status of being its definition.

For even when those [other conditions] are absent, there is no cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); therefore, it is established that cognition itself should not be accepted as the definition of the mark. Thus, the reason possesses only three characteristics.

"The result is as before" means that just as in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the result was stated to be twofold— cognition of the object and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*)— so too here, by stating that the result of inference (*anumāna*) consists of comprehension (*adhigama*) which is non-different from perception, it is implied that inference also has comprehension as its essential nature.

Therefore, he asks: "If both [are the same]," and so forth. The meaning is: "But the object (*artha*)—that is, form (*rūpa*)—is unequal for these two. The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of restriction; it means that while these two [the objects] are indeed unequal, their nature as realization (*adhigama-rūpatā*) is equal.
But surely, the apprehension of those two is their form (*rūpa*).

If that is non-different, then what other form is there that is said to be "the form of these two is unequal"? That which was established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, the conformity (*sārūpya*) with the object—is what was stated to be "unequal."
For it is thus: that [cognition] is clear for perception, but indistinct for inference.
Regarding the passage beginning with "viṣayo hi" and so forth:
by the word *viṣaya* here, the intended meaning is the objective support (*ālambana*), and not the object of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For even in the case of inference, validity—characterized by non-discrepancy—is indeed directed toward the real entity (*vastu*) as its object.
Therefore, due to the difference in their objective supports (*ālambana*), he states that there is a difference in the objects of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But how is there a difference in the objective support?
Because the appearances (*pratibhāsa*) are distinct.
For it is not logical that two dissimilar forms should belong to a single [entity]. Furthermore, the term "different" (*bhinna*) should be understood as a mere negation of non-difference (*abheda*),
and not as referring to a plurality of objects, because conceptual inference (*anumāna-vikalpa*) is devoid of a [real] object.
And that object which is accepted as the domain of inference is, in reality, unestablished.
"And because of the specific form of that.
Here, "that" refers to the object of perception and inference.
Its "form" (ākāra) is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), so called because it is "formed" (ākriyate), that is, determined.
The meaning is that "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) refers to the distinction (*bheda*) of its form.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "particularity" should be understood as being intended to exclude the absence of particularity;
it does not, however, establish a state of manifold intrinsic natures (*nānāsvabhāvatā*), because the universal (*sāmānya*) is a conceptual construction and thus lacks reality.

This is what is indicated: because perception has an external object, it possesses a clear manifestation of that object, whereas inference does not; rather, the indistinct form of the object in inference arises solely from the power of its own seed. Therefore, the nature of perception and inference is distinct as described. Alternatively, for perception, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*) that directly produces its own clear form; for inference, however, that very same [particular] produces its indistinct objective form through a mediated succession.
The object of cognition is [known] through another form.
Others maintain that even perception [is known] through another form.

Thus, since the objects of perception and inference are distinct, their own natures are also distinct by virtue of the difference in their essential character, insofar as they take the form of clear and unclear objects respectively.

(8) Now, as for the question "Why?"—the reason is that he demonstrates through a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) that inference alone is divided into two types based on the distinction between [inference] for oneself and [inference] for others, whereas perception is not.

This is what is meant: why is it not accepted that there is a second type of perception for others, namely, the verbal expression used to make another understand an object that one has personally perceived?
Regarding the phrase "because" and so forth:
for inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object.
And since the very same kind of inference that one has regarding oneself is produced in the mental continuum of another by means of speech, it is logical that it is twofold.

The object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), however, is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). And it is not possible to produce in another mental continuum through verbal expression a perceptual cognition of that [object] which is such as one’s own; for that [particular characteristic] is inexpressible.
Otherwise, even those who are blind and so forth would have from words a cognition of exactly that same kind, appearing with vivid clarity.
Why is it that this [perception] is inexpressible? He says: "Because of the difference from the object of apprehension" (*grāhyabhedāt*).
For the unique object of apprehension (*asādhāraṇa-grāhya*) belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
and that cannot be expressed, because it has never been seen before.
Inference, however, is the opposite of that;
therefore, it is inference alone whose object is to be specified, not perception.
By the phrase "like one's own self," this indicates that the nature of perception and inference is distinct.
This is something to be personally realized by everyone;
and it would not be possible for these two to imitate the form of their respective objects if they were directed toward the same object.
Therefore, just as the intrinsic natures of these two are distinct, so too should their difference in object be understood.
Consequently, the object of perception cannot be specified in the same manner as that of inference.
Others, however, say: "For fear of breaking the meter, that which ought to have been stated later was stated first.

Therefore, the text should be understood as follows: when it is asked why inference alone is divided into two kinds and not perception, he states the reason: 'Because of the difference in the objects of apprehension' (*grāhyabhedāt*), and so forth.

If inference is divided into two kinds because of the difference in the objects of apprehension, then perception too would likewise be divided into two; to this he replies: 'The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible' (*anirdeśyam*)."
This is what is meant: it is intended that such is the object of perception and inference, wherein one is demonstrable and the other is non-demonstrable.
Therefore, it is inference alone that is divided into two kinds—that whose object can be communicated to another by means of speech, but not so perception.

But surely, by the statement "the object and the form of these two are unequal," the distinction between the objects of the two means of valid cognition was already established, and from that distinction follows a distinction in their own natures.
Why, then, is this now introduced: "For the objects of perception and inference are distinct, like their own selves," and so forth?
There is no fault here, for this point was stated previously with one purpose, whereas it is stated now with a different purpose.
With the words "yadi ca" and so forth, he establishes that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible.
The meaning is: it would follow that [the particular] must be inferable by that very word; thus, that very object which is grasped by perception would have to be understood from that word.
But this is not the case;

let it not be that even a blind person or the like perceives that object through direct perception alone. However, the opponent—failing to perceive this fault due to his own dullness, and demonstrating that [the mind] conforms to what is seen because he himself accepts that it has only valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as its object—says "Indeed, it is so for me," and so forth.
It indicates this:
for touch is the object of direct perception, and it is precisely that which is inferred by means of color; so he thinks.
"Sometimes" means when the touch is not being touched by the sense organ;
it does not mean "as in the case of perception.

For perception determines the touch through a form that is established precisely by the exclusion of the consideration of other differences, whereas inference [determines it] through a recollection drawn from previous experience—namely, "this is that..."
"Previously, I perceived this together with this form"—this is the generality of touch, which is distinguished from non-touch.
Regarding the phrase "just as," he provides an example in connection with the recollection of what was previously seen:

just as a form is not grasped through direct perception in its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and thus becomes a logical mark (*liṅga*) only by way of its general aspect (*sāmānyākāra*) connected with what was previously seen—since the particular (*viśeṣa*) does not persist [in the same way].

Likewise, he shows that touch is not to be inferred from its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) simply because it was not apprehended by prior perception; rather, it is to be inferred only in the form of a universal (*sāmānyākāra*), which is suitable for inference.
(11) How is there conventional discourse regarding what has been seen and so forth?
If noble ones engage in such discourse by describing things exactly as they were experienced, then it is appropriate.
However, according to your view, since one perceives a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and then speaks of something else entirely, their conventional discourse would be ignoble.
And consequently, there is a contradiction of what has been accepted.
By the words "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth, he explains this: the words "seen" and so on have as their cause the actions of seeing and so forth.

And these are employed by the Noble Ones (*ārya*) when their respective causes exist, not when they do not; thus, the conventions of the Noble Ones are accepted, but not because of the denotation of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with what has been accepted.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yat tarhi" (then what...), he points out a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*). [He asks:
But surely, it is not the very same moment experienced by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that is experienced by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What then?
It was stated previously that it is "another moment.
How, then, can it be said thus?
This is not a fault.

The phrase "only the object experienced by visual consciousness" is intended to indicate the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); that is to say, it refers to the particular characteristic itself.
Furthermore, because the preceding and succeeding moments belong to the same class, this may have been stated thus with the intention of expressing their non-difference.
Alternatively, this word *anu* functions in the sense of "together with," and the word *bhūta* also means "arisen.
Consequently, the meaning here is that one cognizes an object only as it has arisen together with visual consciousness; thus, there is no fault.

If that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is experienced by mental consciousness is inexpressible, how is it that the mind cognizes blue and that very same [object] as being permeated by verbal expression, namely, "it is blue"?
"In that case as well" refers to the treatise.
"Because it is not known by a name that can be designated through another aspect," and so forth.
An "other aspect" than the aspect of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the aspect of the universal (*sāmānyākāra*).
Therefore, it is not to be designated by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Its name is this designation "blue";
and it cognizes that, not merely the own-characteristic.
Therefore, in the treatise, the mind is held to be twofold.
By the phrase "by the exclusion of the non-blue," he indicates that other form.
It is said to be "by the exclusion of the non-blue" in accordance with the intentions of those who engage in linguistic convention;
for it has been stated that they engage in convention through a determination of reality.
Otherwise, this would be mutually contradictory.
For instance: if one designates the mind by means of another mental aspect, then it is not that very object experienced by visual consciousness which has been designated;
yet, if one designates that very specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), it cannot be done by means of another mental aspect.
Regarding the phrase "even in the case of non-universals":
by the word "even" (api), it is implied that this applies to universals as well, such as impermanence and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having the nature of air and so forth":
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), imperceptible elements such as space are included. As he said:
Kaṇāda:

The connection of this sūtra is as follows—when an opponent has stated that "air is merely touch because it is not perceived like earth, water, or fire," he says this in order to refute it: "We shall establish the cognition of even the unperceived through its inferential mark."
What, then, is its indicative mark? That is stated: "and touch.
Since there is no touch among those things that are perceived, air has an unperceived indicative mark.
And touch is perceived, devoid of the specific qualities of coldness or heat;
by the word "and" (ca), sound, support, and trembling are also included.
In a place where there are no trees or shrubs, the whistling sound of *śuka-śuka* is perceived, as is the support of grass and other such things.
If there were no obstruction by another substance, these would fall due to their weight;
yet their stability in the air is observed,
as is the swaying of creepers and the like.
And this [touch] does not belong to the perceived [elements] such as earth and so forth;
by the word "and" (ca), it is implied that it does not belong to the unperceived [elements] such as space and so forth.
Therefore, because it is not perceived among both the perceived and the unperceived, the specific touch is itself unperceived.
Thus, because its mark (liṅga) is imperceptible, air has an unperceived mark.
Nor was it previously perceived, since it is apprehended for the first time through a specific quality of touch; therefore, this inference has a non-common (asāmānya) object.
"It is not because of the indication of that generality," [meaning] that by the word "that" (tat), only touch (sparśa) is connected, and not air (vāyu).
For this very reason, he says: "Indeed, that [touch] does not exist in air and so forth," and so on.
The fact that touch is dependent is indicated by its being a quality (*guṇa*);
whatever is a quality is dependent, just like odor.
And touch is by way of its qualities;
it is the intrinsic nature.
Alternatively, showing that the word "that" (tat) refers specifically to air, he says: "Nor [is it] in the natures of air and so forth," and so on.
The meaning of this is as follows: whatever is a quality (guṇa) is dependent upon a substance (dravya), like odor;
and touch is a quality—this is its inherent nature (svabhāva).
Since touch is a quality, its dependence on a substance is inferred; from this, its status as a substance alone is established by implication.
The intention is that just as the fact that the eyes and other senses exist for the sake of another is established, the "other" (the self) is also established by implication.
"By way of elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*).
He considers that the establishment by elimination is indeed inference, because it is produced from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
As he says, etc.
This touch does not belong to earth, because it does not coexist with odor and the other qualities [of earth].
It does not belong to water or fire, because it is neither hot nor cold.
Nor does it belong to space and the other [elements], which are unperceived.
For in the case of jars and the like, there would be resistance therein because they possess tangibility;
but this is not so for the mind, because its qualities are inferable.
Its qualities of atomicity and oneness are those which are to be inferred.
But this [touch] is directly perceived.
Furthermore, there exists no quality that is without a substratum.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), this touch belongs to air alone; such is the proof by elimination.
(15) "Not so, because its existence is not established.
By the word "that" (*tat*), wind (*vāyu*) is connected.
For, when something is impossible for others, its existence is postulated there only if its existence is already established.
But for one for whom even the existence [of such an agent] is unestablished, how can it be conceived that he exists by way of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*)?
For when it is conceivable that this effect was not made by some other person present there, it is not reasonable to conceive that it was made by the son of a barren woman by way of elimination;
rather, in those very cases, there arises the doubt as to "by whom was this made?"
"And because the negation is equal. Even if its existence were established, inference is not tenable because the negation is equal.

Just as this touch has not been observed before in earth and the other [elements] and thus does not belong to them, so too it was not observed before in air; therefore, let it not belong to that either.
How, then, is the remaining proof of wind established? He says: "For when [it is] established," and so forth.

Just as the existence of produced things such as jars is established, if the existence of those things under investigation—such as wind—is likewise established, then the reason (hetu) attains its status as being established;
not otherwise.

In the case of consciousness (*citi*), where negation is impossible, even if their existence is established, if that property were sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—just as coldness is in fire—then the reason would likewise remain unestablished; however, it is established through the opposite [of such sublation]. Thus, it has been demonstrated how the establishment of the reason is brought about.
"Due to the connection with a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*). A specific quality is intended here as a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) serving as the reason (*hetu*).
Its "connection" is its inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*).
"Having abandoned the generality of qualities" means having abandoned the generality of properties (*dharma-sāmānya*) which is subject to deviation.

"By means of a specific quality" means by means of a property that possesses the aforementioned existence in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The meaning is that air is inferred by way of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), since an inference regarding a specific substance is being performed.

In this case too, it should be understood as occurring through a general form (*sāmānyākāra*) and not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because the fact that inference has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object was already refuted previously.
The inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*), however, is for the purpose of excluding substances such as earth and the like.

In this regard, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever property of a thing, whose existence is established in something A, is not possible in others than A, and which is not sublated with respect to that [property] by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), belongs to that [A].

For example, impermanence—which is a property of things, impossible for others than those things whose existence is established as having originated—is not sublated by a means of valid cognition in their case. Likewise, the sensation of touch that is neither hot nor cold—which is a property of things, impossible for others than wind whose existence is established—is not sublated by a means of valid cognition in its case; thus, it is an essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Thus, when touch is established as being connected with air by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), air is established in some particular place or at some particular time. However, showing that according to your own view this establishment by elimination is not possible for these [elements], he says: "But existence is unestablished," and so forth.

Since existence is unestablished and the refutation is equal to that of earth and the other elements, the meaning is that there is an absence of specific qualities—that is, an absence of a property possessing the three characteristics [of a valid reason].
Therefore, since there is an absence of any specific quality therein, how could there be inference?
Not at all.
Thus, having first accepted the refutation based on both the seen and the unseen, the absence of inference has been stated.
Now, demonstrating that this very negation is improper, he says: "If [it were established] by mere non-perception," and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*), he indicates that the non-existence of something is established only from its non-perception when it has met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
[Objection: But surely, since touch meets the conditions for perceptibility, its negation is indeed proper.
This is not tenable, because it is merely the visible nature [of things] that is not being negated.

You state your negation having apprehended a generality such as "earth" and so forth. However, since a difference in touch is observed even when that [generality] is present in cases such as cotton, stone, and leaves, and since a particularity may also occur in some instances, one must remain cautious; therefore, it is improper to conclude [non-existence] based on mere non-perception everywhere.
A negation.
Showing that [the production of sound] from invisible [causes] is also not logical, he says: "For not from the invisible," and so forth.
The word *hi* (for) denotes either a conjunction or a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). [The phrase continues:
"Because there is no impact for those that are formless."
This negation must concern either impact (*abhighāta*) itself, or the affirmation of a thing contrary to it.

If it is a negation, then a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or a pervaded-pervader relationship (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) must be stated between impact and the specific kind of touch; for it is only when the cause and the pervader are themselves excluded that they exclude their respective bound effects and pervaded instances, otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, the relations of cause and effect, as well as pervader and pervaded, are not established [in this case], because a specific kind of touch exists even without impact (*abhighāta*), and because [the absence of impact] is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). Now, if by the phrase "because there is no impact for those that are formless" one intends to refer to a real entity called "non-impact" through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), then its connection with space and so forth must be proven, and it must be shown to be in contradiction with a specific kind of touch.
Otherwise, how could that which is unconnected and non-contradictory with it invalidate this [other thing] there? Or else, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
In that regard, a relation is not established. To explain: a relation would have to be either its occurrence in those [atoms] or its being produced by them.
First of all, occurrence is not established, because they are beyond the senses.
For no activity whatsoever is observed in regard to supersensible objects; nor can it be determined that "this [cognition] exists here" without such observation;
nor is its being produced by that [object] established, because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is unproven.
For the capacity of a cause is not understood through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, but rather also through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
And that [negative concomitance] does not exist here, because since space and so forth are eternal and all-pervading, it is impossible for the effect to be absent when the cause is absent.
Thus, in this way, the very entity called "non-striking" (*anabhighāta*), which is related to space and so forth, is not established.
How, moreover, could there be a contradiction for that [ether] with a particular kind of touch?
For instance, jars and other objects do not obstruct sunlight and the like,
yet they possess touch.
Therefore, negation is not established from that.
"And because [the self] is to be inferred from its qualities" (guṇānumeyatvāt).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Furthermore, the genitive case in "in the mind" (*manasi*) is based on the distinction arising from the production of qualities; it does not depend on [the self] being an object of inference.
The meaning of the statement is that [the existence of] qualities of the mind is to be inferred.
Furthermore, because a quality does not require another quality for its own permanence, there is no fault of lacking capacity;
this too is not a valid reason, as there is no contradiction.

For instance: just as the quality called omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the self is inferable while pleasure and other qualities are perceptible, so too the two qualities of the mind—its atomicity (*aṇutva*) and its oneness (*ekatva*)—would be inferable, and this quality of touch would be perceptible;
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Now, in order to establish what is logical in this regard, he says: "What then? and so forth.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

But how is it that [the reason] "because it is seen among those things that are seen" was stated, given that that particular quality of touch is not actually seen even among those things that are seen?
This is not a fault.
For among those things that are perceived, a general property of touch is observed as being accompanied by particular features;
however, regarding those things that are unperceived, there is no observation even of that [general property].

Whatever is observed to possess a common characteristic in a certain place is possible there; for example, a sweet taste is observed in *āmalaka* fruits. And a specific tactile quality is observed among those things that have been seen to possess it.
Alternatively, whatever is observed in a certain place possesses the possibility of specific qualities therein;
for example, taste in myrobalans.
And since touch is observed in those things that are observed, these two are essential natures (*svabhāva*).

In both cases, the qualification "provided there is no sublation" (abādhaka) should be understood. However, in the case of air and so forth, non-perception must be stated in order to negate the conventional usage of "existent.
If this were so, there would necessarily be a certainty that "this [existence] is possible only here."
However, doubt is observed [in such cases]. Therefore, since this [doubt] does not occur among those things that have been perceived, he says: "And of those," etc.
The meaning is that doubt arises because of multiplicity, not because of impossibility in that regard.
Showing that they too have refuted the inferential nature of air (*vāyu*), he says: "By the formulation of the designation 'authoritative' (*āpta-sañjñā-vidhānena*)," and so forth.
The phrase "the inferential nature of air does not [exist]" is to be supplied here.
This refers to the case where there is an inference based on the general category of substance (*dravya-sāmānya*).

Having abandoned the inference of a mere substance— on the grounds that "there exists some substance which this [quality] depends upon, since it is a quality called touch that is dependent on a substance"—
[the author says]: "Because of the authority of the designation of the trustworthy one."

Since those whose defects have been exhausted have established exactly nine designations for substances—among which eight designations have been assigned to the eight substances beginning with earth, and only the designation "wind" remains, and there is no other tenth substance—one understands the existence of wind through the negation of any tenth substance other than earth and the others, as well as any substance other than earth and the rest, such that one concludes: "That of which this touch is the quality is wind. This is not because there is even the possibility of a [separate] distinction [between wind and touch].

In order to refute the claim that verbal testimony (*śābda*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the proponent of another means of cognition first provides the following answer, while he himself will provide further answers later on.
Regarding the phrase "by virtue of what is well-known" (*prasiddhivaśena*):

since the presence [of the reason] in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and its absence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are already established for the listener, there is no need to state an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The mention of the "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is for the purpose of indicating the [other] members [of the syllogism], meaning that the members are not explicitly taught.
This is what is being said: that which has its members not taught is distinct from inference, just like perception;
and thus verbal cognition (śābda) is of the same nature.
"Even so" indicates a deviation [from the rule].
"Of a single example" refers to this.
The singularity of the example is in relation to its remaining parts, but not in relation to [other] examples.
Therefore, the meaning is this: that there is simply no statement of an example at all.
Or, "of both."
The word "vā" (or), functioning in the sense of "and," effects an unexpressed conjunction; the meaning is: "of three, four, and five.
Therefore, even when one employs a common reason (*sādhāraṇahetu*), there is still an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by means of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
This is what is meant by the phrase "the consequence regarding verbal cognition" (*śābdaprasaṅga*).

The meaning is that for another [opponent], verbal cognition (*śābda*) is understood to be distinct from inference (*anumāna*); therefore, the same consequence applies as in the case of verbal cognition—namely, the consequence that it too must be distinct from inference.
That is to say, it follows that this [cognition] is of the same nature as verbal cognition.
For it has already been stated that even without the suffix *-vat*, its meaning is understood.
"But others say," and so forth.
For a word conveys its object as having a form non-different from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas smoke and the like do not.
Indeed, when one cognizes fire through smoke, or when one causes it to be cognized, one does not cognize or cause it to be cognized by way of the form of the smoke itself.
How is there inference regarding an object?
Because an object possesses multiple forms,
is that object apprehended there in its specific form or in its general form?
He considers it to be entirely untenable;

for instance: if words such as "tree" were to convey an object such as a tree by means of general forms such as "existence" (*sattva*), it would follow that all words have a single meaning, because general forms are common to multiple objects.
Now, [if it is argued that] it is incorrect in its specific form because an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) nature cannot be communicated, then there is an absence of the word-meaning in every respect;
[namely,] that the object denoted by the word "tree" does not exist in other things.
Just as for you, the word-meaning is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoḍha*), which is a universal—(22)
"It is the same for me as well.

However, this is the distinction: I have accepted that it is perceived as being colored by the form of that word. This shows that the object denoted by the word "tree" is not something other than a jar or the like.
Due to the absence of any other word-meaning, that portion of the object which is denoted by the word "tree" is indicated here.

This is what is meant: that very portion of the real entity (vastu) which is characterized by the exclusion of other objects is the meaning of the word "tree," because it alone possesses similarity with that [word].
It is not [the meaning] through common forms such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, nor through an uncommon form; this is his view.
The reading of others is that the referent denoted by the word *vṛkṣa* does not become the referent of another word;
the meaning of the word *vṛkṣa* is not the meaning of any other word. The intention is that synonyms, because they possess a single referent, are indeed non-different.

In this case as well, by demonstrating that the referent of the word "tree" is not denotable by any other word, it is stated that the meaning of the word "tree" is simply "treeness" (vṛkṣatva) as characterized by the exclusion of the referents of other words; thus, the meaning remains the same.
But surely, even by the word "substance" (*dravya*), an object possessing branches and so forth is conveyed;
yet that [object] does not have that [word's] form.

Therefore, since it is observed that something is denotable even when there is no similarity of form, meaning is not conveyed through similarity of the word’s form. To this, he says: "Even though," and so forth.

By the word "api" (even/also), he reveals the intended meaning: that the word "substance" (*dravya*) is indeed non-denotative because it deviates from the specific instances of substance; however, the subsequent answer is stated while provisionally accepting [the term]. "Another form" (*rūpāntara*) means another aspect (*ākārāntara*), which is a certain part of that very same entity.

The intention is that there is indeed a formal similarity (*sārūpya*) between that [quality] and the word *dravya*. Furthermore, this was stated—namely, "by the exclusion of non-substance" (*adravyanivṛttyā*)—in order to show that this other form is characterized by the exclusion of non-substance.

"Now, as for the phrase beginning with 'nanu ca' [but surely]: not only is another form of the object—characterized by the exclusion of non-substance (adravya)—understood through the word *dravya* as being fit to attain similarity (*sārupya*) with the word *dravya*, but this is also the case with the word *vṛkṣa*.
For instance, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed: 'the substance is a tree' (*dravyaṃ vṛkṣaḥ*)."
For that [denotative function] is not possible between two things with distinct referents. Nor is similarity (sārūpya) between the word and its object admitted by you.
Consequently, that same fault remains; for even in the absence of similarity, one observes that words have objects.
The intention is that the denotation of an object does not occur through a similarity with the name itself.
That is to say, it is not from the word itself;
rather, that [exclusion] is understood from the very meaning of the word "tree," which is invariably connected with the exclusion of non-substances.
However, the deluded person thinks that it is understood from the word alone.
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), however, arises because that which is accompanied by a qualifier resides in the qualified object;
it is not the case that the word "tree" expresses the exclusion of non-substances.
This is as stated in the passage beginning with "if the words 'tree' and so forth... and so on.
If it were said that only words ending in nominal suffixes (*subanta*) are the basis for the authority of the word, there would be no fault.

For instance, their fully established form (*pariniṣpanna-rūpa*), which is capable of being identified as "this is that" through reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), enters into the intellect; thus, a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the word with that [object] is possible.
However, it is not the case that only nouns (*nāman*) are said to denote fully established objects.
What then?
Even those [words] ending in verbal suffixes are included, as he says: "also by means of verbal words," and so forth.

By means of verbal words such as *pacati* ("he cooks") or *paṭhati* ("he reads"), action (*kriyā*) is expressed—action which is devoid of gender and number, whose parts are arranged in a temporal sequence, and whose own nature is not yet fully established.
Furthermore, it is not possible to apply a metaphorical identity (*abhedopacāra*) to such an object through the intellect if it has not been apprehended as "this is that.
Nor does the nature of the word, which is established in its own form, undergo the state of assuming the form of the [perceived] object.

And for those who hold that the sentence alone is the word (*śabda*), because it denotes the meaning; if the sentence alone is the word, for what purpose is there the employment of individual words? To this he says: "And it is the means for its comprehension," and so forth.
He considers that [the sentence-meaning] consists of the collection of those [words], just as phonemes constitute words.
Regarding the statement "they do not exist," etc.:

for the meaning of a sentence may be external—consisting of the relationship between the goal and the means—or it may be an indivisible action supported by the application of the power of the means; or it may be internal, characterized as *pratibhā* (intuitive flash).
Furthermore, all three of these [factors] are non-substantial (asattvabhūta) and thus transcend the reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) that "this is that.
Nor is it possible to employ the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) "this is that" on the basis of an object that is of such a nature.
Regarding the phrase "a mere trace of distinction":
the failure to state a formal example and the metaphorical treatment of non-difference by means of the word [itself] constitute a mere trace of distinction.

(25) If, then, there is no difference [between perception and verbal cognition], and you, while establishing that wind and so forth are known through scripture (*āgama*), have already established that the object of verbal cognition is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then—since scripture and inference would be non-different—the objectivity of the particular characteristic would be established. To this he says: "In that regard, [the object] is devoid of words," and so forth. "In that regard" (*tatra*) means in the treatise (*śāstra*), with reference to the treatise.
This is what is meant: you accept that your treatise has particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Therefore, this inference—namely, "and touch," "nor is there touch among those things seen," and so forth—which was put forward, is stated by you yourselves to have non-particular characteristics as its object, precisely because of the reason provided in your own treatise.

He asks: "With what intention was this said—that 'being based on scripture' (āgamikatva) is established for you alone, and not for yourself"? He replies: "Intending the mark (liṅga) that is independent of verbal testimony. This means that this mark called "touch" is abandoned by the word known as "scripture," because it establishes the existence of air independently of that [word].

Thus, having in mind that the logical mark (*liṅga*) accepted by you is ineffective according to the authority of your own treatise, I have stated that the inference arising from it has as its object what is not a specific characteristic (*asvalakṣaṇa*). However, [you might argue] that verbal cognition (*śābda*) itself does not likewise have the specific characteristic as its object; therefore, in order to demonstrate this, he says: "But verbal [cognition] also... and so forth.
"Absence of a relation" refers to the time of the convention (*saṅketa*).

For one who understands the relationship between word and object perceives from the word only the generality of the object experienced at the time of the convention, and not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because that was not previously seen.
At the time of application, there is no possibility whatsoever of suspecting that it has a particular as its object.
However, at the time of the convention, since the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is perceptible, there arises the possibility of suspecting that [the word] has that as its object;
therefore, he states that there is no connection [between the word and the particular].
That which has a visible object (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is that in which the object is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the opposite is that which has an invisible object (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Regarding the visible object, there is the acquisition of the linguistic convention (*saṃjñā-vyutpatti*).
For example, in the case of "This is a jackfruit tree" (*panasa*), there is only the acquisition of the relationship [between name and object], not inference, because the object is perceptible.
Regarding objects that are not perceived, such as heaven (*svarga*) and the like, there is merely a conceptual construction of the object.

For words such as "heaven" do not project the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of heaven or similar things into the intellect, either at the time of linguistic convention or at any other time; otherwise, it would follow that they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Rather, when employed by those intending to communicate them, these words project an image of the object whose nature does not appear to the listener, such as: "There exists some particular excellence of fragrance belonging to the gods."

And in this way, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is neither apprehended nor demonstrated; for if it were, there would follow the consequence of a difference in appearance, just as occurs for those who have actually experienced heaven and so forth upon hearing about them.

Furthermore, even while not apprehending its true nature, one is satisfied by determining that very [nature] within a conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimba*), because the comprehension of the word-meaning consists precisely in being of such a nature.
And here, the absence of a [necessary] relationship is not what is required;
rather, it concerns only those things whose objects are perceived.
For in those cases, since the specific feature is actually perceived, one might suspect that it alone is the denotable meaning.
Then, for the purpose of avoiding that [objection], it was said: "the derivation of the designation."
How, then, is that [scriptural cognition] an inference?

The intention is as follows: one seeks out scripture with the thought, "Having ascertained through scripture some supersensible object useful to a person, and acting accordingly as appropriate, may I attain [the goal].
Therefore, if there occurs merely a conceptual construction of an object and no cognition of a specific object, its status as inference is indeed lost.

But surely, just as in the case of words uttered by an unreliable person, their status as inference arises solely from the expression of that mere object which is characterized by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), and not from the denotation of an external object, so it should be for words uttered by a reliable person as well. To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: the authority of the speech of a reliable person is not to be accepted as residing in the mere intention alone, but rather also in the external object.
Otherwise, what would distinguish it from the speech of an unreliable person?
Therefore, by words such as "heaven" employed by a reliable person, only the mere object is expressed.
What then?
An external object is also unique to worldly linguistic usage.
The scriptures are not inferences merely because they express specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
What then?
They are [inferences] because they manifest objects through a general form (*sāmānyākāra*), producing nothing but conceptual constructions (*arthavikalpa*) of that kind; and therein—(28)
Showing that [the word of a reliable person] is not deceptive, he says: "Because of the commonality of non-deceptiveness with the speech of a reliable person," and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is that the word of a reliable person, which has as its object things that are entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), possesses the nature of inference because of its commonality of non-deceptiveness with other words of a reliable person whose objects are things perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).

But surely, because words have no necessary connection with their objects and because it is impossible to ascertain the excellence of a person, it is improper to grant validity to [scriptures] regarding external objects.

This is true. However, the intention here is this: a person is not able to remain without relying on the authority of scripture (āgama), because one hears of certain great benefits and calamities resulting from [actions] whose fruits are beyond the senses, and because no contradiction is observed in the existence of those [benefits and calamities].
And: "Since one must act when there is something to be done, it is better to act in this way.
Therefore, he states that validity [is established] through critical examination.

In this regard, that treatise which is capable of demonstrating the human goal and its feasible means is worthy of examination; it is precisely that which should be examined, for it is improper to apply one's attention elsewhere. If, when put into practice, it does not become subject to contradiction, it would be excellent.
(29) "Having grasped the word of a reliable person," and so forth.
Having grasped the word of a reliable person as the cause for attaining non-discrepancy, its status as inference has been stated.
Why, then, is its status as inference explained? Because it is equal to [inference] in terms of non-discrepancy with the object.
What, then, is its non-contradiction?
It is the state of being as it is for those things intended to be perceived directly, and the state of not being perceived for those not so intended;
likewise, it is the state of being as it is for those things intended to be objects of inference, and the state of not being inferable for those that are not so.
This non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the complete purification of all objects that can be definitively determined.

Its general character is inferred even regarding an object inaccessible to perception and inference, upon observing its status as the word of a reliable person (*āptavacanatva*): "Whatever is the word of a reliable person is non-contradictory, like other words of a reliable person;
and there exists some word whose subject matter is entirely beyond the senses."
It is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Consequently, even though scriptures do not take the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, they are authoritative not merely with respect to the speaker’s intention— as is the case with other words—
but rather with respect to the actual object as well.

Alternatively, the status of the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*) as inference is stated on the basis of its non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*). Non-contradiction is the non-perversity of what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, and the means thereto, as taught by him.

Thus, because this [word] is non-contradictory regarding that which is useful for human goals and fit for practice, one may conclude that it is likewise [non-contradictory] in other matters; it is not for deception, because there is no obstruction [to truth], and because for the speaker, the utterance of useless falsehoods would be fruitless.

(30) Thus, having no other recourse, the inferential nature of scripture has been described in both ways—[the former] being preferable because it results in activity [based on scripture] rather than activity [based on inference].
Indeed, inference in this manner is not free from error, because words do not possess an invariable concomitance (*anāntarīyakatva*) with their objects.
In this context, non-discrepancy is inferred by taking the word of a reliable person as the basis.
Once that [non-discrepancy] has been inferred, the status of the reliable person’s word as inference subsequently arises from that very non-discrepancy.
Furthermore, the term "inference" (anumāna) here refers to the inferential mark (liṅga), because it is by means of this that one infers, or because it is the cause of the inferential cognition.
Furthermore, the non-deceptiveness of the authoritative word (āptavacana) is due to its being directed toward a purposeful object;
moreover, that [purposefulness] follows from the intention of the cognizer, and not from the power of the thing-in-itself.
By the phrase "for it has been said thus," he harmonizes his own view with another treatise:
trustworthy persons, having apprehended the nature of heaven and so forth through direct perception, apply designations.
Furthermore, the act of applying a designation should be understood as being merely illustrative.
For indeed, they all speak only after having first perceived the object;
otherwise, they would not be authoritative persons (āpta) at all. Therefore, every word of theirs is non-contradictory.
And for this reason, it is inference.
"By this direction," it is said;

since there is no perceived relationship with the Pradhāna and so forth, one must state—following the previous argument—that the Pradhāna and other such principles are merely derived from scripture (*āgamika*), because their indicative marks (*liṅga*) are not observed [in the world].
(31) "In the object of inference and in what is similar to it. The word "atha" has the sense of conjunction; the meaning is "and in what is similar to it.
Furthermore, this should be understood as an illustration for positive concomitance (*anvaya*), namely that [the reason] exists in what is similar to it.
Just as in the expression "Let the curd be protected from the crow," the term "crow" refers to any destroyer such as a dog or the like;
this is what is meant: positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the second characteristic [of a valid reason].
And in this way, the threefold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason "audibility" with respect to impermanence is established, but not otherwise.
For there is no existence of that [the probandum] in what is similar to it;
however, positive concomitance (anvaya) does exist. For positive concomitance is indeed the existence of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) in the mark (liṅga).
And that [invariable concomitance] exists for the property of audibility.
For instance: wherever there is audibility, there impermanence necessarily exists;
otherwise, we shall demonstrate that audibility itself would not be tenable.

In the phrase "non-existence is non-being" (*nāstitāsatī*), it should be understood that by the word "non-being" (*asat*) not only is an absence equivalent to that [object] expressed, but also something other than it and its opposite, due to the exclusion of its form.
Alternatively, "non-existence" (*nāstitva*) should be seen as indicating difference (*vyatireka*).
And the meaning of the sentence is that difference is the third form.

(32) In this case, since the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) alone are already established, their status as the object of inference (*anumeya*) is untenable. Furthermore, as for the aggregate (*samudāya*), it is simply not possible as long as the property has not been established;
for a property-bearer qualified by a property that has not entered into the intellect is not logically coherent.
But once the locus (*dharmī*) has been established, the composite [subject] arises afterwards;
at that time, its status as the "probandum" (*sādhya*) ceases because it has already been established.

Therefore, anticipating the objection of someone who claims that the existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the object of inference (*anumeya*) is simply impossible, he says: "For the object of inference... and so forth.

In this context, although the word *dharma* denotes a general category, nevertheless, because the discussion concerns the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it refers specifically to that for which the means are sought; due to proximity, it applies precisely to that.
What, then, is this?
It is the *dharma* whose specific characteristics are the object of inquiry.
For no wise person would present a proof for a property (*dharma*) of a subject (*dharmin*) that has not been sought to be known (*ajijñāsita*).
Therefore, when a proof is adduced regarding a subject whose existence is established, that very property which was sought to be known is what is signified by the word "property" (*dharma*).
By this [qualification], the object is distinguished as being excluded from other things; such is the meaning.

Consequently, this is the very meaning that follows: the subject (*dharmin*) is that which is qualified by the specific property sought to be known (*jijñāsitaviśeṣa*). For instance, when something is qualified by a particular feature that one wishes to know, that feature becomes the "property sought to be known" for that subject. Even the statement that "the aggregate (*samudāya*) is the probandum (*sādhya*)" is to be understood precisely with reference to the property sought to be known.

(33) Others maintain that the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) is indicated by means of that property which is established at a later time; however, at the time of perceiving the mark (*liṅga*), there is no qualification by the property because the property is not yet cognized. Since the context concerns the "indicative" reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*), it is determined that cognition is implied by the object [of the reason]; thus he says, "In that regard, perception," and so forth.
In this context, "there" refers to the object of inference (*anumeya*). "By perception" (*pratyakṣataḥ*) refers to smoke and the like.

For one who has perceived by means of direct perception a location accompanied by smoke as having a form distinct from other things—that is, in its unique, specific nature—it is by the power of that very perception that there arises a certain cognition whose object is the particularity as it was seen, in the form: "This is that very same [place]."
The inferential knowledge of a mark (*liṅga*) arises at a later time;
however, that is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it does not apprehend an object capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-yogya*) that has not already been apprehended.
Only the first [cognition] is a valid means of cognition, because of the opposite being the case, since this is the defining characteristic of a valid means of cognition.
Why is this so?
Because the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has reality as its basis.
Why is that also so?
Because the activity of a seeker is directed toward an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),

it should be understood by this that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), its properties (*dharma*), and so forth, lack validity. Consequently, those who raise the objection that the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and the like must constitute a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is not included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), merely reveal their own stupidity.
"Or by means of inference" means that [the nature of the object] is inferred through marks (liṅga) such as being produced or being occasional.
The phrase "at a later time" is connected to each [of the preceding terms]: namely, at a later time than perception, or at a later time than inference.
Furthermore, the word "inference" here refers to the cognition of the mark (liṅgajñāna).

As it has been said: "Because both of these are causes of inference either directly or through a succession, both are 'inference' (*anumāna*), having taken the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the agent (*kāraka*).
[This refers to] "the property (*dharma*) in its general form."
The apprehension of the universal form is for the purpose of excluding the specific form, because [otherwise] inference would be impossible.

Nor can that [universal] be made an object by a cognition following upon perception and so forth, because that cognition is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), and conceptual cognitions have universals as their objects.
"And in that which belongs to the same class" (*tajjātīye ca*).

Here too, it should be connected with "in a general form" (*sāmānyarūpeṇa*). [Objection: But surely, there would be a contradiction in the property-possessor (*dharmin*) as qualified by its specific attributes occurring elsewhere; or, if it were not so qualified, it would not possess the status of being a property of the inferable (*anumeya-dharmatā*).
This is not so, because the qualification is by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), as in the case of "Caitra is an archer.

If, then, a specific feature of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) is useless for the practice of inference and the object of inference, and thus only the universal (*sāmānya*) is accepted as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then that same [universal] must also be grasped for the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); for its specific feature is likewise not useful in that context.
And if it were a proof of a universal, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
This is not a fault;
for the universal itself is the probandum by way of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedena*).
Nor is this a case of proving what is already established, because the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda) has not yet been proven.

By mentioning "a portion" (ekadeśa), he demonstrates that even a reason which does not pervade the similar instances (sapakṣa) can still function as a valid reason (*hetu*). He asks, "Why is this so?"— that is, he questions on what basis it is understood from the statement regarding the existence [of the reason] in both the object of inference and its similar instances that in one case it exists everywhere [in the similar instances], while in the other case it exists only in a portion.

(35) Since sentences have exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as their fruit, and because restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended [by the speaker], this [meaning] is obtained; thus he says: "only similar to that" (*tattulya eva*), and so forth.
By this, he shows that the restriction here is based on the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), as in the example: "Pārtha is the archer.
If it is argued that [this would mean] the reason does not occur in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), we say no, because its purpose is the negation of [connection with] others.

In that context, once the *vṛtti* (the commentary) has been obtained, the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) being conjoined excludes something else; for instance, [in the phrase] "he first begot two sons of his own, Nara and Nārāyaṇa," it is thought that [the particle] need not be stated at all,
because its meaning is already understood from that very restriction.
Regarding the phrase "this, moreover," and so forth:
that by which something is restricted is called a *niyama* (restriction).
A formal argument (*prayoga*) is said to be either one possessing similarity (*sādharmya*) or one possessing dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

For when one reveals the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by means of a formal argument (prayoga-vākya), the intellect of others— having mounted the swing of doubt as to whether this [cognition] is eternal or not— is established as being exclusively non-eternal by being excluded from other possibilities;
thus, the formal argument is a restriction (niyama).
For that purpose, a third characteristic must be stated.

Since even a single characteristic whose positive and negative concomitances possess a certain pervasion implies the second by implication when it is employed, there would be the employment of only one;
thus, the logical mark (liṅga) would result in having only two characteristics.
It is not [a case of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) having separate forms;
rather, since these two can be demonstrated by a single sentence, it is called a "combination of application" (*prayoga-samāsa*), not a "combination of form" (*rūpa-samāsa*).
For it has been said: "Because both are shown by one or the other through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*)."

It might be argued: "Non-existence is not at all possible in the absence of an existent, because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), since causal factors (*kāraka*) are indeed characterized by their capacities (*śakti*), and what is non-existent lacks all efficacy. To this, he says: "Non-existence exists precisely in the absence [of existence].
The particle (*nipāta*) is displaced in its order [in the compound].
It should be viewed that when something is non-existent, it is simply non-existence;
or else, let it remain exactly as it was previously stated.
If this is so, it follows that non-existence does not obtain for that which possesses existence.
This is not a fault; for in this defining statement, "non-existence is non-existent," the restriction is intended to mean that there is simply non-existence of non-existence.
Thus, non-existence is described as being subject to a specific rule.
It was with reference to this that it was said as follows.

This is its meaning: when something is non-existent, there is only non-existence, which takes the form of the negation of the object, and not existence in the form of a positive injunction, because a positive injunction is incompatible with non-existence.
This is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Not elsewhere" means:
since "non-existence" was the subject immediately preceding, it should be understood here as having a different meaning in relation to that.
In something other than non-existence—that is, in that which possesses existence—there is not merely non-existence, because affirmation is also possible therein.
By this [statement], one who negates the existence of a non-existence that possesses a restriction implies the meaning that there exists a non-existence devoid of restriction.
For through a qualified negation, a cognition of its opposite arises, just as in the example: "There is no fruit on this *palāśa* tree.
This is an example because it is established for the opponent.
For when the other does not exist, one does not desire non-existence; but when it exists, one certainly does.

(37) But what is the reason that non-existence is restricted [only] when something is absent? He says: "not contradictory. The particle *iti* indicates the reason. This shows the following: if some property of a real entity (*vastudharma*) were to be predicated of a non-existent thing, there would be a fault, because a property of a real entity cannot possibly exist in what is non-existent.
And nothing at all is being enjoined here;
rather,
a mere negation is being made.
Furthermore, the non-existent, such as the son of a barren woman and so forth, is not contradictory to non-existence;
therefore, that [non-existence] is possible in that regard.
Whatever is not contradictory to non-existence is possible therein.
For example:
the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not incompatible with non-existence, which is characterized by the negation of the properties of a non-existent thing.
However, legal proceedings such as those concerning ownership and so forth are not based solely on the actual state of things;
the intention is that even the opponent, by asserting "it does not exist when it is absent," has already admitted this.
"Grasping of knowledge," and so forth.
That by which knowledge is grasped is "grasping of knowledge," which is another effort (*yatnāntara*).
This is what is meant: one must apply such another effort that the knowledge whose object is the *liṅga* (probans) is obtained.
Otherwise, there would be an inference of fire and so forth in a specified particular location even from smoke and the like that have been cognized otherwise [than as being in that specific place].
By the statement "knowledge also is acquired," and so forth, he shows that since knowledge is implied by the force of the context, it is not something to be established through a separate effort.
(38) "Having one, two, or two forms," and so forth.
That which possesses one and two forms is described as such.
Here, the masculine gender is used due to its connection with the referent (*artha*).
"By way of meaning" (arthataḥ):
this shows that even without the word, this meaning is obtained through implication.
If, then, this meaning is already established by implication, for what purpose is it stated?
By stating, "This meaning has been established by me through the sense of the words even without explicit verbal expression," it becomes as if it were explicitly stated;
yet, the restatement of what is already established by implication does not bear fruit.

This is true; nevertheless, for the sake of instructing those of dull intellect, this meaning—which is already implied—is explicitly stated, but not with a view toward those who possess innate understanding.

Here, an objection is raised: by the phrase "its existence is exactly like that," a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is being established, and that cannot occur without negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also expressed by the phrase "non-existence when [the other] is absent.
Yet even that does not occur without positive concomitance (*anvaya*). How then can it be said: "It exists in what is similar to that, and it does not exist in its absence"?
"In its absence it does not exist, nor does it exist in what is similar to it," and so forth.
This is not a fault;
for these definitions of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) were not stated with reference to the essential nature (*prakṛtarūpa*) [of the probans].
What then?

It is merely the presence [of the reason] in the similar class (sapakṣa) and its mere absence from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), devoid of any necessary restriction. Words may proceed according to one's whim, but the actual state of affairs must be examined.

And this is the meaning intended here: that which lacks positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not a logical reason (*hetu*), even if it possesses the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
And that which lacks the property of being a feature of the subject is also not a logical reason, even if it possesses positive and negative concomitance.
Furthermore, this can indeed be demonstrated by this very method as well.

Regarding the statement of non-reliance (*anāsthāvacana*): according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, the argument "sound is eternal because it is corporeal" is of a single form, by way of comparison with eternal and corporeal atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Likewise, the argument "sound is eternal because it is not an object of cognition" is of a single form, due to its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
The argument "sound is eternal because it is incorporeal" is of two forms and is common (*sādhāraṇa*).
