"Sound is eternal because it is audible"—this is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason with two forms, provided that soundness (śabdatva) is not accepted as eternal.
"Sound is non-eternal because it is visible"—this is an unestablished (asiddha) reason with two forms, provided that universals (jāti) are not admitted to be perceivable by the eye.
There are also [inferences] that are formless (arūpa). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is visible," and so forth.
However, such cases are not mentioned in the *Vṛtti*, as they are understood by this very same method.
In the Sūtra, however, regarding the phrase "each one [is] of one or two forms," the word *ca* (and) should be understood as having the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of those [forms].
Others, however, say: "The formless (*arūpa*) is not mentioned because it lacks the status of being a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).
For whatever possesses even a single part of that [form], appearing as such, causes a reversal of cognition; therefore, only that is mentioned here."
(40) For it has been stated that the object of inference is the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by a property (*dharma*).
He introduces the following passage, beginning with "But here," in order to refute the views of those who maintain otherwise.
The term "because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārataḥ*) refers to the reason (*hetu*).
That for which the non-deviation [of the reason] from something is not stated is not the probandum (sādhya) of that [reason]. For example, water is not the probandum of smoke.
And since the non-deviation of the reason from the property to be proven is not stated, they consider this to be the nature of the negative-only (vyatirekin) inference.
"Because it is established":
that which is established is not something to be proven, just as "fire is hot.
Furthermore, [the opponent] states a contradiction of essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*) by asserting that both the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) are already established.

"If the logical mark (liṅga) is established in relation to the property (dharma)" means that whoever intends to prove only the property must necessarily observe the logical mark in that very [property];
otherwise, it would not cause that [property] to be understood.
For a mark known in one place does not cause another [place] to be cognized, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Consequently, since the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is already understood at the very time the mark is perceived, what else could remain to be inferred for the sake of which the relationship would need to be remembered?
Now, in the phrase "in a place connected with fire," the inclusion of the term "connected" (*sambaddha*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for the word "that very" (*sa eva*), it is used to exclude the possibility that the mere property (*dharma*) itself is the probandum (*sādhya*). Why, then, is that very place not accepted as being "possessing fire"? [The answer follows:
It is for the sake of excluding the status of the mere property as the probandum. (41)
In this way, the property alone (*dharma*) is appropriately connected as the object to be proven (*sādhya*), provided that the locus (*dharmin*) is not intended as its substratum.
Otherwise, if the substratum were accepted as that locus wherein the logical mark (*liṅga*) is perceived, then the composite whole (*samudāya*) itself would become the object to be proven;
therefore, that [composite] must be what is intended.
This must necessarily be accepted as such.
For if only a property (*dharma*) were to be proven, its existence (*sattā*) would also have to be proven;
and that is incorrect, because that [existence] is already established. As it has been said: "For it is not the case that the existence of fire is not cognized."

By this, he states the previously mentioned [reasoning] regarding the contradiction of essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*), beginning with: "That which is established is not that which is to be proven," and so forth.
"Even in the case of a relation, the dyad does not exist.
The dyad refers to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the property that proves (*sādhanadharma*).
For fire and smoke do not both exist within a relation characterized by conjunction between the fire and a particular location.
If duality does not exist there, why is it that [the locus] does not become the probandum (*sādhya*)? To this he says: "And thus it is done," and so forth.
For at the time of inference, inference is performed by means of the two words "where" (*yatra*) and "there" (*tatra*), which refer back to the object of inference (*anumeya*).
In this case, if the location (*pradeśa*) were the probandum, its reference by those two words would be appropriate.
Otherwise, if fire and smoke were indicated by their own names [as the subject], then even the location would not be the object of inference.

Furthermore, since the two [fire and smoke] would not exist in the relationship [between them and the location], those two [the relationship and the location] would be rendered devoid of a locus. Therefore, he states the following, which is pervaded by a contradictory [reason]: "That place where fire and smoke do not exist is not to be inferred by means of smoke, like water; and neither fire nor smoke exists in the relationship. Thus, he expresses that which is pervaded by the opposite.

(42) "The genitive case would have been heard"— for if there were an intention to express a relationship, the word *agni* would have ended in the genitive, as in the expression "the touch of fire is hot.
However, what is actually heard is "fire is here," where the word ends in the nominative.
Then it is calculated: "No relation is intended here.
But surely this is the section on inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
In that case, what occasion is there for the genitive case?
This is not a fault.

By the absence of the hearing of a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), [the author] clearly perceives the lack of a relation in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) and thereby demonstrates it even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
This is what is meant: where the word "fire" (*agni*) ends in the nominative case, there is no intention to express the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a relation.
For example, when the word "fire" (agni) is employed without the intention to express its grammatical relationship—
as in the phrase "the fire here" (*agnir atra*) where it ends in the nominative case— the word "fire" is incompatible with its function [as a term requiring a specific syntactic relation].
It might be argued: "The relationship has already been expressed by the locative case ending itself;
so why would there be the contingency of using the genitive?

In that case, what would be the solution when the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) are used with nominative endings, as in the expression "sound is impermanent" (*anityaḥ śabdaḥ*)?
When it is said, "There is no fire here," the relationship of locus and located is not understood as something to be established;
rather, what is understood is simply that there is no fire at all.
And since that which is connected [to the reason] is what is being proved in a particular location, it follows that that very collection (samudāya) is the probandum (sādhya).
It cannot be expressed by its own nature, because a relation is defined as a connection;

since the word "relation" denotes it as a positive entity (*bhāva*), and a positive entity is joined with another related term, there arises an expectation for another correlate: "Of what is this the relation? (43)

Consequently, since that [relation] exists only as something related, the relation is not denoted in its own right; nor can it be an object of inference. Thus, he states a contradiction with what has been accepted:
for by one who desires the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) to be a means of proof (*sādhana*), it must be accepted that the object of inference (*anumeya*) is expressible.
If that [object] were to be inferred through its relation [to the cognition], then [the status of being a means of knowledge] would be lost.

If it is not denotable by the word, how then is it cognized? To this he says: "It would be apprehended through the meaning. By the word "fire is here," the location is conveyed as having fire as its locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
And since the location possesses contact with fire, it has the capacity to function as a locus.

Therefore, that very [locus] which is being perceived causes the cognition of conjunction because of its invariable concomitance; thus it is said to be "understood through the sense" (*arthagṛhīta*), since its locative capacity is inferred from its own effect.
[Objection: But in that case, it would simply be an object of inference (*anumeya*). [Response:

There is no contradiction, because what is intended to be excluded for it is its being established by a probans such as smoke, and not its being excluded from being established by every possible probans.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that "the relationship is to be inferred from its own effect"—that too was stated because it is to be inferred from its own effect, and not because it is to be inferred from a probans such as smoke.
This is what is meant: even if there is indeed a connection, it is inferred by its own effect alone and not by another [effect] such as smoke.
As it has been said: "But it is not inferred by means of smoke.
[This refers to] "from the previous reasons."

Even if there were a relation, duality would not exist; furthermore, the genitive case would be heard [in the word "relation"], and [the self] would be inexpressible as possessing that [relation]. For these reasons, [it is not so].

(44) And this [fire] is not "conjoined with the mark" (*liṅga-saṅgata*); the meaning is that it is not connected with the mark by way of a relation characterized by inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
That which is not demonstrated to have inseparable concomitance with something else is not inferred by means of that [other thing], just as water is not inferred from smoke.
And the inseparable concomitance of smoke with [fire] has not been demonstrated by way of such a relation.
[The reason] is pervaded by the contradictory [property].
As for its non-demonstration, it is because there is no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with that which is not its effect, since that would be a different matter (*arthāntara*).
With the words "This is not... and so forth, he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
The phrase "in another place" refers generally to all locations such as a kitchen and the like.

For what purpose is this shown? It is because the logical mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, which is well-known in a particular location and so forth where fire and the like are intended to be proven, is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with that property—namely, fire—and is thus connected to the locus (*dharmin*), such as that specific location.
For the purpose of [the verb] "will go."
"But in another place" refers to the generality of a location possessing smoke.
"In another place," and so forth: this word "in another place" (anyatra) applies to the locus (*dharmin*) that is the probandum (*sādhya*), such as a specific location.
Regarding the phrase "even upon seeing mere smoke":
the word *mātra* (mere) is for the purpose of excluding the sight of fire; its meaning is "even when fire is not seen.
Alternatively, by the word *mātra*, he shows this: that it occurs even without the observation of a concomitance (*anugama*) with the subject (*dharmin*).

This is the summarized meaning: although the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by its property (*dharma*) is what is to be inferred, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of smoke with fire that is demonstrated in places such as a kitchen serves as the very means for establishing that a particular location possesses fire.
For it is thus: from the certainty that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," one perceives mere smoke elsewhere and thereby understands the location to be possessed of fire.

Therefore, the state of being necessarily inseparable from the property (*dharma*) must be demonstrated. Now, this inseparability might be demonstrated either with respect to a specific subject (*dharmī*) or with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*).

In this regard, it cannot first be demonstrated by way of a specific instance, because that would be impossible due to its not having been cultivated elsewhere; as he said: "For otherwise," and so forth.

However, an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is possible by way of the generality of the subject (*dharmin*), and that is what is demonstrated by him; as he said: "But by way of the generality of the locus (*ādhāra*)," and so forth.
When an inseparable connection is shown by means of the contained (*ādheya*), it is also shown by means of the locus, because the locus is dependent upon the contained.
Alternatively, by the statement "where there is smoke, there is fire," it is not expressed that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire in general;
rather,
it is [concomitant] with fire as qualified by its locus in general.
Therefore, that [invariable concomitance] has indeed been shown even by means of the generality of the substratum (*ādhāra-sāmānya*).
However, because there is no demonstration whatsoever of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) by way of a [specific] relation, it was stated: "This is an unequal presentation.
Thus, the intended reason is precisely this: the failure to demonstrate invariable concomitance even in a general sense.
And since it does not occur in its opposite, there is no inconclusiveness.
"But the investigation regarding the property (*dharma*) is different.

Previously, the investigation concerning the object of inference (*anumeya*) was stated; now, however, the investigation concerning the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is presented, and it is demonstrated by means of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
The word "tu" (but/however) indicates the possibility of such an investigation.

Furthermore, that investigation occurs only in the case of the sign (*liṅga*) and the sign-bearer (*liṅgin*), which, like the subject (*dharmin*), possess multiple properties—just as fire and smoke do—for the purpose of determining the aspects of the signified and the signifier;
it does not apply, however, to cases such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*).

In that case, since it is impossible for there to be multiple properties [in a single entity], the doubt as to by which part the relationship of the signifier and the signified could exist simply does not arise.
"Exclusion of that which is concomitant":
it is called "concomitant" (anubaddha) because it follows along.
That aspect which follows the fire, such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth—it leads to its exclusion, that is, its differentiation (vyāvṛtti), from other heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa).

He asks: "What, then, are the specific conditions that are invariably concomitant? and replies: "Those without which fire does not exist. But surely, since smoke is the indicator, one should say "those without which smoke does not exist.
Why, then, does he speak in this way?
There is no fault here, for this very same meaning is expressed by way of this formulation;
for instance: without those [causes] fire does not exist, and even smoke certainly does not exist without them.
Alternatively, the phrase "those which are connected" should be construed as "those which are connected specifically to smoke.
To demonstrate precisely those things that are connected to smoke, he says: "without which," and so forth.
For it is only those [things] without which fire does not exist that are connected to smoke.

Regarding the statement that it causes those things which are connected [to it] to be excluded from others, he provides an example: "as [the cognition] of fire [induces] the mere exclusion of non-fire.
To the question, "Why does it convey a mere exclusion and not a specific [positive] attribute? he replies: "Because of its conformity with its own connection," and so forth.
This is a causal reason (*kāraṇahetu*), not a logical mark (*liṅga*).

For he says that this [reason] conforms to its relationship by stating, "it is not observed anywhere in what is non-fire"; by this, he demonstrates the predominance of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) through its non-observation in every instance of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
And he says, "it is observed elsewhere as well."
By the word "api" (even/also), it is indicated that [the connection] is not seen in some cases, thereby showing that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is subordinate.

Thus, since the relationship has negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as its primary element and positive concomitance as secondary—and since that [relationship] is possible only in a general sense, not in a specific one—it is for that reason, in accordance with that [nature], that [the statement] expresses, by way of negative concomitance, merely the exclusion of non-fire, namely: "fire here is not non-fire," and not [something else].
Just as there is a connection by way of being fire, so too there is a connection by way of substantiality, quality-ness, and so forth;
thus, it establishes the very exclusion of non-substantiality and the like for those [qualities] as well.

He states another reason for the claim that a logical mark (hetu) leads to comprehension by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*): "By means of the properties of being a quality (*guṇatva*), odor (*gandha*), fragrance (*saugandhya*), and its specific varieties," and so forth.
"By the increase of one" means by the increase of each one individually.
[The phrase] "by means of being a quality, [it is distinguished] from non-substances (*adravya*)" [is explained as follows].
In the statement "This is a substance because it possesses quality," the exclusion of non-substances is effected by means of "quality" with respect to things such as lotuses.
For instance, that [quality] is not observed anywhere in non-substances, whereas it is observed in substances.
In that exclusion of non-substances, there is an initial increase by one, in relation to which the exclusion is effected by an increase of one through "odor."
However, it is stated as "not a substance" (*adravyāt*) for the purpose of demonstrating that [quality].

For this very reason, qualityhood (*guṇatva*) also functions as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) toward the exclusion [of substance] by means of the single increase [of the suffix -tva]. For if the exclusion of non-substances were indeed effected by that [term *adravyāt*], then the exclusion would be effected by the single increase [of the suffix -tva] in "fragrance" (*gandha*), and not otherwise.
And thus, in this verse, it is not contradictory for the word *guṇatva* to be included within a *dvandva* compound, as it is of equal status (*tulyakakṣyatva*) with the other words.
[This is seen] in the phrase "from what is not earth and from what is not a substance by virtue of being smell-ness" (*gandhatvena*).
By the statement "this is an earthly substance because of smell-ness," an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is made both from what is not earth and from what is not a substance.

"By fragrance, from what is common to both fragrant and non-fragrant. This means that by the term "fragrance," there is an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from both the preceding [categories] and from what is common to the non-fragrant.
Here, "common to the fragrant" (*surabhisādhāraṇa*) refers to the general property (*sāmānya*) shared with the fragrant, namely, the mere state of being odor (*gandhatvamātra*).
That which lacks a common fragrance is described as such; the meaning is that it is odorless.
A "specific fragrance" refers to particular scents such as those of the blue lotus (*utpala*) and so forth.

Thus, the exclusion of non-substances and the like is observed to be effected by properties such as *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality) in the case of the blue lotus and others, through an incremental increase [in the number of excluded categories].

How is this logically tenable? If the reason (hetu) causes cognition by way of the exclusion of the contrary (vipakṣavyāvṛtti), but not otherwise—as is observed—then indeed, because the perception of all [reasons] by all [persons] would be indistinguishable when viewed through the lens of affirmation (vidhi), the resulting cognition would be identical in every case.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the reason leads to understanding solely by means of exclusion.

To those who do not accept this, he says: "Like what is seen" (*dṛṣṭavat*), and so forth. "Like what is seen" means equal to what has been seen; that is to say, if it were to manifest [the object] in the same way as the mark (*liṅga*) was previously perceived at the time of establishing the relationship—namely, by way of affirmation, such as "fire is here"—it would not be [an inference]. (49)
By way of its function: "Only fire is here, not non-fire.
Thus, it should be understood that because [the object] is not perceived everywhere, there would be no manifestation; for it was previously stated, "one should manifest."

"If indeed [it is argued] that 'as it is seen in fire,' etc."—if the proponent of the positive injunction (*vidhivādin*) were to accept this, namely, that "because smoke is seen only in fire and not in the absence of fire, therefore it makes [the object] known," then the manifestation would occur solely by way of negation (*pratiṣedha*).
Therefore, he must accept it in this way: "Because it is seen only in fire and not unobserved, therefore it makes that [object] known."
And therefore, one should not state it at all;
for it has not been observed in every fire, since it is impossible to observe it in every instance of fire that differs in direction, location, and so forth.
The phrase "if, moreover" introduces another fault.
For when smoke is seen in fire, it is seen as necessarily associated with one or another of its specific qualities, such as being blazing;
consequently, it would also manifest those qualities.
But it is not so.
Therefore, mere perception is not the cause for the cognition of an inferable object, because even when that perception exists, the [cognition] may be absent.
Now, one might object: surely perception is also accepted by the proponent of negation.
For instance: smoke is the logical reason (*hetu*) for fire because it is invariably concomitant with it as its effect.
And the causal relationship is established by both perception and non-perception combined, not by non-perception alone; thus he says, "Since...
and so forth. He demonstrates this: because smoke [indicates] fire... (50)

It manifests only in its general form, not in its specific forms such as "flaming" and so forth; therefore, for the sake of establishing the relationship between cause and effect, it is understood that even by means of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), only that [general] form of it is perceived, and not the specific form, because the latter is not the cause for the establishment of the causal convention. For the perception of specific features such as "flaming" is not the cause for the establishment of the causal convention, since smoke is observed even in the absence of those [specific features].

If it is argued that the relationship of producer and produced exists only in part, we say no; for this is accepted in the case of perceiving a specific quality produced by that [cause], but it is not accepted in the case of perceiving an undifferentiated universal, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

It might be argued as follows: "The universal entity exists as one and the same in the individuals, whether it be distinct from them or non-distinct. And because it is fully present in its entirety within each individual, its perception is possible in even a single instance of fire. Therefore, the claim that 'because it is not seen everywhere, there can be no manifestation [of it]' is incorrect. To this, he says: "Even if the universal... and so forth.
By the phrase "even if," he shows that such a thing does not exist at all,
but that the fault is stated merely for the sake of argument.
To begin with, fire-ness does not exist.
If the universal were something other than the individual, it would appear as distinct in cognition; yet it does not so appear.
Therefore, its existence being negated by the non-perception of its own nature, it simply does not exist.

Now, if it were non-different [from the individual], even so, that universal would not exist, just like the individual. Nevertheless, having provisionally accepted [the existence of the universal], he says "Even though that exists," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the impossibility of perceiving it.

That which is common to multiple substrata and whose entire set of substrata has not been apprehended cannot be perceived, just as duality and so forth cannot be perceived when their entire set of substrata has not been apprehended.
And such is the nature of fire (*agnitva*).
This is a contradiction of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
Nor does it belong to similarity [itself].
Since similarity is not distinct from its substratum, it has been presented separately.
Here too, this very same argument should be stated.

Now, even if it is grasped as a single substratum, it is nonetheless grasped in its entirety. This being the case, because it is fully present in each instance with its whole nature, it would follow that it is multiple, like a quality (*guṇa*).
For this possibility does not exist: that which is fully present in one place with its whole nature could also be so in another.
Whatever is fully present in each of several places with its whole nature is multiple, like a quality.

And likewise, the universal (sāmānya) is the essential nature (svabhāva) [of that which is excluded]. Since the whole (avayavin) is also negated by this very [reasoning], there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
Moreover, because it would consist of many [individuals], that universal would not even exist, just like its substrata;
for a universal is held to be one.

With the words "tathā" (thus) and so forth, he demonstrates the investigation into the logical mark (*liṅga*) previously proposed. It is called a "mark" (*aṅga*) because by it the object of inference (*anumeya*) is marked (*aṅgyate*) or understood; it is called a "logical mark" (*liṅga*).
"It does not transcend" means that it does not deviate [from the object].
"Even though there are manifold dharmas" means by way of general and specific dharmas.
"By means of smokiness, paleness, and so forth.
Here, "paleness" is intended specifically as that which is related to smoke, and not as that which resides in curd, rice-pudding, and the like, because of the latter's deviation [from fire].

[Objection: In that case, why does it not cause cognition through "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and other such properties as well, when these too are apprehended as being adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) of smoke?
(52) It indeed causes certain cognition; there is no other possibility here.

However, this was stated with reference to the apprehension of an undifferentiated universal: "not by means of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth," but rather "by means of smokeness (*dhūmatva*), paleness (*pāṇḍutva*), and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), specific qualities such as pungency and so forth are included.
He summarizes the very point already stated in two summary verses for the sake of easy comprehension: "They too are understood through the mark.

The meaning of the word "too" (*api*) is that those concomitants—such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth—are also understood, and not only properties such as fire-ness (*agnitva*), which is what one intends to cognize at that time. [The phrase] "erroneous" (*vyabhicāriṇaḥ*) refers to the mark (*liṅga*).
Its variability [as a logical reason] depends on distinctions such as being "blazing" and so forth.

However, the meanings that are connected with the *liṅga* (the inferential mark) are the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which are undifferentiated;
whereas those that are differentiated are smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) and so forth.
And these are called "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) in relation to the general properties such as substantiality, but not in relation to their own unique, specific form.
Now, as for the objection that "it resides in both": every relation indeed resides in two things, and its operation upon those two related entities occurs without distinction.

Consequently, just as there is no distinction between two conjoined things in their state of being conjoined, so too there would be no distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*).
And thus, the generality of the mark would be the indicator, and the particularity of the bearer of the mark would also be the indicated, because the relationship is without distinction.
Whatever two things are based on a single relation, they possess identical properties, like the two conjoined things.
And likewise, the mark and that which possesses the mark;
[this is] the semblance of essential nature.
As for the claim that "a relation resides in two things," a relation does not reside in two things at all.
For instance, a relation is simply the state of being inseparable (*avinābhāvitva*).
And that [reason] exists only in the mark (liṅga), not in the bearer of the mark (liṅgin).
However, having granted for the sake of argument that it resides in both, he shows that the subsequent [response] is stated given their coexistence,
by means of the analogy "like the container and the contained."
The occurrence of that relationship between the mark and the bearer of the mark is like that between the container and the contained, and not like that between two conjoined objects.
"Never a support," and so forth.
The property of the supported is its dependence upon the support for its stability;
the property of the support is the establishing of the supported.

He states the inconclusiveness [of the reason] by saying that even though the substratum (*ādhāra*) and the superstratum (*ādheya*) share a single basis for their relation, they do not possess identical properties;
thus he says, "never," and so forth.
The meaning is that the signified (*liṅgin*) and the sign (*liṅga*) do not possess each other's properties.
With the words "But the conjoined," and so forth, he states the dissimilarity between the sign (liṅga) and the signified (liṅgin) by means of two examples of conjoined things.

With the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that the property of being the locus of a single relation is unestablished, thereby reaffirming the very relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) previously stated.
For instance: the relation between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
And this [concomitance] resides only in the mark, not in the bearer of the mark; this is established by these two restrictive determinations.
How so?
Because the possessor of the mark necessarily exists in the mark.

How is this restriction (avadhāraṇa) appropriate? If it means that "wherever there is the mark (liṅga), there the marked (liṅgin) exists," then the occurrence of the marked elsewhere is not prohibited by this, because the purpose of the restriction is merely to exclude its absence from the mark.

Consequently, it is stated that the state of being invariably concomitant (avinābhāvitva) does not exist in the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), because its presence is indicated even elsewhere than in the mark itself.
Just as the nature of fire exists in smoke, so too do [properties] such as substantiality (dravyatva) exist;
therefore, smoke is an indicator of those [properties] as well, but not of [qualities] such as brilliance.
For those [properties] do not necessarily exist in smoke; as he said: "Therefore, it is logical," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the phrase "the other, however, only in the possessor of the mark" (liṅgin), he indicates that the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) operates only in the case of the mark (liṅga); for the meaning understood is that the mark does not exist elsewhere than in the possessor of the mark. However, the existence of the possessor of the mark elsewhere than the mark is not prohibited.
Just as the property of being smoke (dhūmatva) necessarily exists in fire, so too do specific properties such as paleness (pāṇḍutva) and the like.
Therefore, those [specifics] are also indicators (gamaka), but not [general categories] such as substantiality (dravyatva).
For these latter do not necessarily exist in fire, as he said: "Therefore, it is logical," and so forth.
With the words "For thus," and so forth, he explains the second half [of the verse].

(55) But surely, previously the existence of the mark (*liṅga*) in the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) was stated, based on the statement "its existence in what is similar to that"; whereas here, the existence of the possessor of the mark in the mark is stated, based on the statement "the possessor of the mark exists in the mark.
How then is there no contradiction?
This is not a fault.
When the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) reside in the same locus, just as the bearer of the mark exists in the mark, so too does the mark exist in the other.
This is stated merely to demonstrate that the relationship resides in the mark alone, by way of reversing the restriction.

If, then, it exists only in the mark (liṅga), how was it stated that the relationship is between the mark and the marked (liṅgin)? Although it exists only in the mark, it is stated thus because it exists in relation to its counter-correlative, the marked; it is not because it resides in both, so there is no fault.

By the passage beginning with "nanu ca" and so forth, he refutes what was stated—that the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) exists only when there is a restriction—and demonstrates that inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) also exists in the case of the bearer of the mark.

With the words "Granted" (*kāmam*) and so forth, [the author] shows that although a mark (*liṅga*) may indeed exist in some way within the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), it exists only in the form of the possessor of the mark itself.

Thus, demonstrating that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) resides in impermanence precisely as a reason (*hetu*) in relation to the probandum (*sādhya*) of "being produced," he establishes his own position.
He further states: "The mark is also pervasive."

It is "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) because it pervades. Regarding the term "possessing the sign" (*liṅgin*), this refers to impermanence. Since that quality of pervasiveness has as its object the possessor of the sign, it is said to be "pervasive in the possessor of the sign."
For example, as in the case of "the gambler among dice.
However, in that instance, it is due to pervasion (*vyāpti*);
for if there were impermanence, the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) would indeed be pervasive.
Therefore, because it is pervasive (*vyāpitvāt*), the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is merely that which is to be understood (*gamya*), not that which makes [something] understood (*gamaka*).
To the question "In what way?", he says: "Like a cow's horn.
Just as a horn, because it is pervasive of the cow, becomes merely that which is to be understood in relation to the cow and not that which makes [it] understood, so it is in this case.
Whatever exists in a certain place is an indicator of that [place];
for example, "cowness" is an indicator of "possessing horns.
And "being produced" necessarily exists in "impermanence."
Intrinsic nature.
"Why is this so? he asks, doubting the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
[The answer begins with] "By the non-occurrence of the object to be negated," and so forth.
The "object to be negated" (*pratiṣedhya*) is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) to the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
In this context, "non-existence" refers to the non-operation of the reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, it is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mark (*liṅga*) which is required and relied upon, because only that constitutes the state of being a reason by virtue of its capacity to produce cognition (*gamakatva*).

Consequently, the meaning is that the pervasion of the mark with respect to the object of the marked (*liṅgin*), even if it exists, is not the cause—that is, not the instrumental basis—for the capacity to produce cognition.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the state of being produced" (*kṛtakatvasya*), etc.:

although the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) pervades all impermanent things, its capacity to indicate [impermanence] does not derive from that quality of pervasion; rather, it derives from the negation of permanence.
Negation of permanence means its non-occurrence therein.
The capacity to convey [the probandum] belongs to that very [reason] alone.

For a reason that is not excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) does not convey the probandum, just like "knowability" (*prameyatva*). Likewise, it applies to the case of impermanence (*anityatva*), and so forth.

When impermanence is adduced as a reason (*hetu*) for the sake of establishing the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), even though that impermanence pervades all produced things, it does not function as a prover by virtue of that pervasion.
What then?
It functions by means of the negation of non-production; that is to say, by its absence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), which is the state of being unproduced.

Thus, since the probans possesses the capacity to indicate [the probandum] precisely through its exclusion from the opposite of what is to be proven (*svasādhyavipakṣa*) and not otherwise, it follows that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) over the object "impermanent" excludes the possibility of non-producedness (*akṛtakatva*). Because there is no room for impermanence in non-producedness—and because [impermanence] would be unstable and impossible therein—producedness is understood through impermanence by means of the negation of non-producedness, that is, by the exclusion of the non-produced.
The expression "by the negation of non-producedness" is intended to exclude the notion that [the probans] indicates [the probandum] through a positive formulation (*vidhimukha*).

But it is not the case that [the reason] possesses the capacity to prove [the probandum], because pervasion through the non-existence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is the cause of its capacity to prove.

And there is no pervasion of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) by "impermanence" (*anityatva*) through the non-existence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance. For instance, when the pervasion "whatever is impermanent is produced" is demonstrated, the exclusion of "producedness" from the permanent is not understood.
What then?
Because impermanence is not produced (*akṛtaka*).

Therefore, since impermanence itself has no scope in the case of being unproduced, it is understood precisely through the negation of being unproduced that being produced is conjoined with impermanence; thus, it is said that [impermanence] possesses the quality of being a signifier (*gamaka*), and this summarizes the meaning already stated.
He composes [this] with two verses.
"Because that which perishes is produced," and so forth.

Since the pervasion of the impermanent by being produced is established, the meaning—that what is not produced is not that [impermanent thing]—is understood even though it has not been explicitly stated. The particle *iti* is indicated here as being elided.
However, that very absence of permanence which constitutes impermanence as the subject under discussion is not demonstrated in the object "produced" by means of that pervasion.
To clarify this very point, he provides an illustration with the second verse: "It would remove the state of being hornless" means it would bring about the state of having horns;
"it does not remove the purpose of a cow" means it does not accomplish the purpose of a cow.
(59) "The perception of an object that is inseparably connected [with another] is inference for one who knows that [connection], because it is by means of this that the [object] is inferred.
An object which does not exist without another is its *nāntarīyaka* (inseparable), such as smoke in relation to fire.
The perception of that [inseparable object] is inference, on the grounds that "by means of this (*anena*), [the object] is inferred (*anumīyate*)."
The cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), however, is the result.
By this, the observation of a deviant [sign] is excluded.
To show that the observation of the logical mark (*liṅga*) depends upon the recollection of the relationship (*sambandha*), the phrase "of one who knows that" (*tadvidaḥ*) was stated.
Inference belongs to one who knows that this [reason] is inseparable from that [probandum], and not to anyone else.
"Only by way of being inseparable (nāntarīyakatvenaiva). For its very inseparability constitutes its own form.
It need not be stated [that it belongs] "to one who knows that," because this is already obtained through the force of the context (sāmarthya).

For it is not possible to have the cognition that "this [word] is invariably concomitant with that [object]," unless the particle *iti* is employed; indeed, the particle *iti* is indicated here even though it is elided,
because without it, the fact that the word has its own form (*svarūpa*) as its referent would not be understood.
The meaning would be that something entirely different from that which is known [to others] is not to be spoken; this is the understanding of the sense.
"Nirdeśa" means that which is pointed out. That whose indicated [portion] is elided is described as such.

The elision (*lopa*), however, consists simply in the non-appearance of that word when its own form is intended to be conveyed; for "elision" is defined as the non-appearance of what was expected to appear. By this, he indicates that one should understand the phrase *tadvidaḥ* (of those who know it) to mean "that which has its own form as its meaning.
As for the particle *iti*, although it would have been appropriate to specify its meaning here, it was not mentioned for fear of breaking the meter.

If it is to be stated by something else, one must specify "how" and "where," because that [vision] possesses manifold aspects. It must be explained by which aspect the seeing occurs and in what location.
For if that were not stated, there would be no restriction regarding the location.
And thus, because visibility is observed in a jar, one understands impermanence in sound as well.
Is it not the case that even regarding the previous alternative, it would have been equally appropriate to raise the objection, "In which [instance] is there perception?
Why then is this objection raised only here?

He thinks as follows: when perception occurs through invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatva), it is understood—even if not explicitly stated—that perception occurs precisely in that [object] without which it does not come to be, because of its proximity to that object.
The term "object" (*artha*) is superfluous; that is to say, the inclusion of the word "object" is redundant.
For indeed, that which is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) is necessarily an object.
What, then, is the purpose of including the word "object"?
Therefore, it should be understood that the word "that" (tat) is used for the purpose of qualifying perception.
By this, inference is the grasping of the form of the logical mark (liṅga).
Now, one might object: since one's own mental form is subject to deviation, inference by means of it is not possible.
He thinks as follows: the apprehension of an object consists precisely in its apprehension in the form of smoke and so forth.
Otherwise, because it would follow a universal (sāmānya), this would be a mere apprehension;

and consequently, the apprehension of the object would be in vain, since the mere apprehension of the object's form is already obtained through the necessary concomitant apprehension [of the universal].
"And the subject under discussion is the *sādhya*. This means that in the context of investigation, the intended object is the *pakṣa* (the thesis), or else,
as in the statement "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the expression of the *sādhya*," it is understood that the observation [of the reason] must pertain to the *sādhya*.

"What is the use of the former?"— this refers to the statement that "the perception of an object belongs to one who knows the invariable concomitance. For when one understands that smoke and the like do not exist without fire and the like, for such a knower, that very perception of the object constitutes the perception of its invariable concomitance.

Alternatively, when it is said "those who know the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*) [have] the observation of the object," the meaning understood is "those who know the invariable concomitance of that object which is observed in the probandum.
And if this is so, what is the purpose of the previous mention of "invariable concomitance" (*nāntarīyaka*)?
Regarding the phrase "and in the case of fire, etc.":

since fire, seed, and impermanence are cited as examples of what is to be inferred (*anumeya*), it is understood that it is the mere property (*dharmamātra*) that is intended to be the object of inference.
For it will be stated that these three examples are distinguished according to their temporal states, such as being present and so forth.
Furthermore, this distinction [of the subject] is not possible when the subject qualified by a property (*dharma*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), because the subject exists in all cases.
Consequently, when smoke and the like are perceived in relation to fire and the like, fire and so forth are already ascertained; what else, therefore, could be inferred for one who knows that?
By this, he states the impropriety of the claim that "the perception [of the reason] occurs in the probandum."
(62) How does one know that which has not been stated? By this [question], the fault of non-elucidation is also indicated.
(63) Regarding the passage beginning with "Of the Naiyāyikas," etc.:

Having first enunciated that "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), and having stated the definition of perception, he next states the definition of inference, as its opportunity has now arrived, with the words "That which is preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*), etc.
That which has the aforementioned perception as its antecedent is described as such.

That [inference] is preceded by perception (pratyakṣapūrva) in which, previously, both the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), or their relationship, have been established through perception; subsequently, one infers the bearer of the mark from the mere sight of the mark. Thus, it is preceded by perception.
"Similar to the former" means "as before.

Just as an object was apprehended through perception at the time of establishing the relationship [between the sign and the signified], so too at a later time, knowledge arises regarding that same object from the observation of the sign.
Therefore, that [inference] is "as before" (pūrvavat).
The *śeṣavat* object is that which is equal to what is perceived by the remainder (*śeṣa*).
The cognition whose object is that [remainder] is also called *śeṣavat*.

For example, having directly perceived the taste of one fruit, one infers that the remaining fruits have the same taste because they are equal to it in terms of their perceived taste; this is the inference of taste.
But surely, that which is other than perception is the *śeṣa* (the remainder), not [the inference called] *śeṣavat*.
Therefore, how can knowledge whose object is that [perception] have as its object the *śeṣavat*?

[Response: Residualness (*śeṣatva*) is mutual dependence; thus, even perception is a *śeṣa* in relation to the other [inference]. Since the other is likewise so in relation to it, there is no fault in [calling] it *śeṣavat*.
Alternatively, "pūrvavat" refers to the cause being prior. That which possesses this [cause] is the effect, which is "pūrvavat.
Knowledge that has this as its object is also "pūrvavat," namely, the inference of the effect from the cause.

The remainder is the effect. That which possesses this [effect] is the "remainder-possessing" (śeṣavat) cause. Knowledge whose object is that [cause] is also "remainder-possessing," which is the inference of the cause from the effect.
*Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is that [inference] which is the cognition of something entirely imperceptible through the similarity of one thing to another;

for example, having observed Caitra’s arrival at another location as being preceded by movement, one infers—by analogy with that—that the sun’s arrival at the mountain of setting is also preceded by movement.

Since the number three is already established by the very mention [of the term], the inclusion of the word "threefold" (*trividha*) is for the purpose of making known the threefold nature of the *pūrvavat* inference, insofar as it has objects belonging to the three times.
In that regard, from the swelling of a river one infers "it has rained" concerning the past;
from the movement of ant eggs one infers "it will rain" concerning the future;
and from the cry of a peacock one infers "there is a peacock here" concerning the present.
In this case, since the state of being preceded [by something] is not possible with the possessive suffix *matup*, it must be construed with the suffix *vati*.
The relation is not perceivable by the sense organs;
for it is considered that, like the qualities of the elements, it does not appear as distinct from its relata.
Whatever does not appear in sensory cognition is not perceivable by the sense organs, just like the sense organs themselves.
And thus is the connection:
the absence of the pervader.
Nor does it apply to all cases, because it is impossible for the sense organs, such as the visual consciousness and its faculties, to apprehend [everything];
the inclusion of the term "all" is intended to show that [perception] is possible through direct perception in the case of fire, smoke, and so forth— by this, he expresses its lack of pervasiveness.
Alternatively, the meaning is that in all cases the two related terms are imperceptible; for its nature as a universal has been established as being imperceptible.
Consequently, because it is impossible [for such a relation to exist], this is not a valid definition.

Nor is it the case that the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) are both perceptible; for even though the intended meaning is understood by this much alone, the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception of some who believe that fire, smoke, and so forth are perceptible in all instances.

It is not the case that [the three types of inference] are possible for everyone, because while one [type] is indeed "prior-like" (*pūrvavat*), it is asserted that the other two do not possess that quality.
And that [inference] is sublated by a previously established [perception];
and this [sublation occurs] by means of another relation. "Another relation" refers to a specific type of relation, namely *avinābhāva* (inseparable concomitance).
By means of that [inference], the object is apprehended as before;
because it is not explicitly stated, inference remains indeed unstated.
In that case, let this [suffix] be *matup*.
Nor does it entail the aforementioned fault,
for not every inference has as its object an effect derived from a cause.

Furthermore, the relationship here is indeed indicated by the demonstration of the nature of cause and effect; therefore, he says: "The possessive suffix *matup* [is not used] because of its fallibility.
For through the relation of cause and effect, there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) only of the effect, not of the cause.
To illustrate: even when the cause is present, the effect may not occur due to the absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
Just as, even when a cloud is present, rain does not fall for farmers due to the absence of merit (dharma),
and even when other causes are assembled, [the result] is obstructed by an opposing factor such as demerit (adharma).
(66) But surely, only a seed or the like that has reached a specific state possesses primary causality;
and it is impossible to create an obstruction to that [state].
So how could there be any deviation? No.

If it is maintained that the cognition of the effect arises from the perception of that [cause] while depending on the recollection of the relationship, then at the time prior to the recollection of the relationship, the effect itself—having already arisen—would have to be perceived.
However, when the effect is not perceived, there can be no comprehension of such a cause from which the effect might be inferred.
Therefore, the establishment of the effect does not proceed from the cause.
With the words "even if there is a remainder" (*śeṣavaty api cet vatiḥ*), etc., he points out here as well the very same fault just mentioned.
For it is not an absolute rule (*na hy avaśyam*) that [a substance] possessing a similar form and so forth must necessarily possess a similar taste. This is not a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*).
This much, however, may be the case: that these [things] have such an intrinsic nature, possess causes similar to those [of the subject], and have such a taste.
But an inference cannot be based on mere similarity of form, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
"If [the suffix] *matup* were [used], it would not occur when there is no understanding," and so forth.
"Non-understanding" (*agati*) means non-comprehension.
Of what?
Since this inference of a cause is based on an effect as the logical reason (*liṅga*),

there would be no cognition [of the cause] if the effect were not perceived, because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of the mark with the object of inference— the cause— would not have been grasped;
yet such cognition is indeed observed.

(67) But surely, the determination of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) occurs precisely through the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between distinct entities. Therefore, how can invariable concomitance be determined without apprehending the state of being an effect? [Response:

What is intended here is the transgression of the state of being an effect as perceived in the treatises (*śāstra*), and not the transgression of the state of being an effect as established in common worldly experience; thus, there is no fault.
For in the treatise, the parts of a stream of water are produced by homogeneous water atoms alone;
however, clouds, by serving as the instrumental cause for the attraction of those atoms, receive the designation of being the "cause of rain"—such is the established position.
Yet the world does not perceive such a relationship between cause and effect.
What then?

Since rain is observed when clouds are present and is not observed when they are absent, one determines the causal relationship through these very observations and non-observations that water and the like are the direct causes of rain. However, a causal relationship as seen in the scriptures is not tenable at all, because eternal atoms are unestablished; even if they were established, they could not be drawn forth due to their immutability; and even if they were drawn forth, [the production of effects] could not occur either successively or simultaneously.
Because the undertaking of an action is impossible, and because a composite effect existing as a real entity has been refuted at length elsewhere by the wise, enough of this digression.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "because of being produced, etc.," he states that the position involving the possessive suffix *matup* is non-pervasive (*avyāpin*). For there is no relationship of cause and effect between "being produced" and so forth and "impermanence" and so forth.

The view of others is as follows: when one part of a single whole, such as the body, has been apprehended through perception—such as the abdomen—the other part, such as the back, is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
Knowledge whose object is that remainder is *śeṣavat* [inference].
And that [inference] does not deviate;
for a belly has never before been perceived without a back and so forth.
Here too, there is indeed the possibility of everything.
For in every instance of inference, the object of comprehension is indeed distinct from the object of perception.
Indeed, no inference ever arises from a mark (*liṅga*) that has not been apprehended.
Furthermore, there is certainly the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as for example, even when parts such as horns are present, parts such as a tail may be absent.

Regarding the phrase "and also as in the case of the former": in the context of the suffix *-vat* in the term *pūrvavat*, when one infers the object "cow" by means of a mark such as its horns, the relation is *samavāya* (inherence).
And that [relation] is described here as being ascertainable through the mark of the cognition [of the object].

In this case, since a relationship with that [universal] is not established for the cognition, and because there is an absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is no application of the logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, it is not established by means of that [cognition].
Consequently, the inference of the object "cow" from the logical mark consisting of the dewlap and so forth would not occur;
yet that [inference] is observed.

For instance, those who investigate through reasoning that "a cow" consists of parts such as the dewlap which depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), ascertain the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and thereby perform an inference of the object "cow" from the mark (*liṅga*) of the dewlap and so forth.
In the inference of fire from smoke, the relation is conjunction (*saṃyoga*);
if even that were not apprehended, there would be no cognition [of the probandum].
And that [conjunction] is indeed perceived; for instance, having seen mere smoke, fire is inferred preceded by the ascertainment of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Yet, at that time, conjunction is not specifically determined as having all its substrata grasped, because—like duality and so forth—it is common to multiple objects.
(69) But in the case of the suffix *matup*, the connection between clouds and so forth with rain and so forth is one of cause and effect.

If the suffix *vat* is used even in the case of the *śeṣavat* [inference], then according to the view that it is *vat*, the co-inherence (*ekārthasamavāya*) of color with taste is as previously stated;
this is because it was presented at the end.
That is to say, the *matup* suffix alternative is the conclusion of the investigation, and this [case] was presented therein.
And regarding the relation of "causality" and so forth:

if a relation between causality and the like with effectness and the like is desired by way of the state of being a mark (*liṅga*) and a marked (*liṅgin*), then because causality and the like depend solely upon effectness and the like, the cognition of the marked object would consequently take on the form of effectness and the like alone,
and not the form of rain and so forth.
He asks, "What is the reason? and replies with the words "by means of the mere relation," and so forth.
For the knowledge of the probandum (*liṅgin*) does not arise from the probans (*liṅga*) without a relation.
And the probans, in whatever way it is related to something, indicates that very thing and nothing else; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And since clouds and so forth are connected to rain and so forth by way of being causes and so forth, and [rain] to them by way of being effects and so forth, there would be a cognition of only those [specific factors].

(70) It might be argued: "The relations such as cause-and-effect and so forth exist between them in their entirety (*sarvātmanā*), not partially; therefore, this undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) does not apply, since even the particularities (*viśeṣa*) possess relatedness. To this he says: "And the apprehension of all aspects," and so forth.
There would also be an apprehension of rain consisting of large drops, accompanied by lightning, and so on; for [the object] stands in a relation of cause and effect with these aspects as well.

For us, however, although there is in every respect a relationship between the produced and the producer, this undesirable consequence does not apply, because it is impossible to determine [the object] in such a manner.
Furthermore, for the opponent, perception is held to be determinate (*niścayātmaka*), and its object is partless (*anavayava*).
Therefore, if that [perception] apprehends it, it must be apprehended by it in its entirety, or else not at all; this has already been stated.
Therefore, this fault belongs to him alone.

Regarding the faults previously mentioned—namely, that there would be comprehension through another relation, that there would be inference from mere effects and so forth, and that there would be the apprehension of all aspects—he states [the following] in order to extend those [faults] to the *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* [type of inference] as well:
"The *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* is also thus."
To the question "How so?", he says: "For that too," and so forth.
Then, what is the distinction of this [cognition] from the two preceding ones? To this he says: "It is absolutely beyond the senses" (*atyantaparokṣa*).
The phrase "and in all cases" refers to the three types [of inference] mentioned previously, namely *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and so forth.
By stating *pūrvavat* and *śeṣavat*, it is declared that inferential knowledge (*anumeyajñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that very [knowledge] is the apprehension of the object (*arthādhigama*).

And there is no other fruit [of cognition]. Consequently, there would be a contradiction of your own tenets. It might be argued: "The cognitions of abandoning, acquiring, and indifference are the fruit."
This is not so, because those [aversions] are caused by the recollection of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
For they do not arise in anyone who does not remember that "this very thing was beneficial" or "this was harmful," and so forth.
It might be argued: "We simply do not accept that there is a result [of karma]. To this he says: "And not... and so on.
That which is the instrument is [the cause] with respect to the action, as it is the fruit of the activity, like an axe;
and likewise there is inference [of this],
which is its essential nature (svabhāva).
Anticipating the objection that [the reason] would be proving what is already established, he says: "The cognition of the mark," and so forth.

The designation [of the inference] as "pūrvavat" or "śeṣavat" would not be established, because it has been explained that only the object of inference is primary in the case of the "pūrvavat" and "śeṣavat" cognitions, while the cognition itself is so designated only figuratively due to having that [object] as its domain.

Furthermore, the cognition of the mark (liṅga) does not have that [object] as its domain, such that this [cognition] could be designated in that way; for since the mark is not described in the treatise as being "pūrvavat" or "śeṣavat," there would be an abandonment of the accepted position.
With the words "And that which... and so forth, he states precisely the abandonment of what has been accepted.
For it was stated in that very same [text]: "It is said to be 'threefold' for the purpose of making known the threefold nature of each one.
What is the reason?
"This very [point]— 'because of the apprehension of the three times'—
this too is not tenable under the view that [the suffix] *matup* [expresses possession], because it is precisely the future effect that is apprehended from the cause. (72)
Nor can it be by means of *śeṣavat* [inference], because inference regarding the future is impossible;
for indeed, the existence of an effect prior to its cause is not possible.
Pakṣila, however, says: "The establishment of sound as a quality follows from the negation of [the other] categories such as substance; this is an inference *śeṣavat*.
Even here, because no relation (*sambandha*) is specified, it is difficult to maintain that this is indeed an inference; how much less, then, can there be its threefold division?
It has already been explained at length—starting with the formulation of the term "authoritative person" (*āpta*)—that the status of sound as a quality is based on scripture (*āgama*).
Therefore, the cognition of the quality-ness (guṇatva) in sound is not inference.
And it is not the case that "it is so there";

for in an inference based on what has been previously perceived (*pūrvavatt*), there is no indication of a relationship at all. Therefore, since its status as an inference is not even specified, how can it have a threefold division?
For it is not the case that [the object] is indicated merely by the statement "it is similar to the preceding," since [the term] "as before" is also employed in the context of memory and so forth.
Likewise, in the case of the statement "it is similar to the remaining perception," no relation whatsoever has been indicated.
(73) This applies also to the Vaiśeṣikas, and so on.
The connection [of this section] is as follows: the rule for the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis has been stated.
Now we shall speak of that which is inferential (*laiṅgika*). He asks: "What is this so-called inferential?"
It is said: [perception consists of] the determination of what has been observed and the following after what has been observed.
Among these, that which is the direct observation of objects—such as "this is indeed a cow" or "this is indeed a horse"—is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, that which is the following after one thing having observed another is not inferential (*laiṅgika*).

However, for the sake of establishing the necessary restriction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), a conventional definition is formulated for that [mark] which would otherwise lead to over-extension.
"Conventional" (*sāmayika*) means existing within a convention; the sense is that it is produced by convention.
For example: "this belongs to that," and so forth.

He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) with the word "of this" (*asya*), and the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) with the word "this" (*idam*). Indeed, when for someone this [effect] is well-known and free from doubt—namely, that "this is the effect to be manifested or produced by this cause which is capable of making it known or bringing it about"—then, upon the observation of that cause, there arises a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) regarding the effect, even though it is not being perceived at that moment; as, for example, from the sight of the rising sun, one has the awareness of the manifestation of a jar.
Having seen the threads arranged as the warp and the woof, presided over by the weaver, in the cloth that is yet to be;

(74) Thus, when this [cognition] of his has become established and free from doubt— namely, "this is the cause of this effect," whether that effect is manifested (*vyaṅgya*) or produced (*nirvartya*)— then, following the observation of that effect and so forth,
it should be stated as appropriate.
The related term is of two kinds: that which is conjunct, as smoke is to fire, and that which is inherent, as a horn is to a cow.
That which inheres in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*) is also of two kinds: an effect [inhering] in another effect, and a cause [inhering] in another cause.

In this regard, the "inherence in the same object" of a cause refers to its inherence in objects located in a single locus; whereas for an effect, it is the inherence [of that effect] in one among several objects—such being the distinction in their grammatical analysis.
Among these, inference from an effect to another effect is, for example, [inferring] touch from color; and from a cause to another cause is, for example, [inferring] the hand from the foot.

The contradictory [cause] is of four kinds. (1) That which is non-existent is [the cause] of that which is existent; for example, the absence of the action of raining is [the cause] of the existing conjunction of wind and clouds, because when that [conjunction] exists, the action of raining is absent. (2) That which is existent is [the cause] of that which is non-existent; that same action of raining, being present, indicates the cessation—that is, the absence of activity—of that very conjunction of wind and clouds. (3) That which is existent is [the cause] of that which is existent; for example, fluidity is [the cause] of the construction of a dam.

By means of flowing, which is the effect of fluidity (*dravatva*), the contradiction with fluidity itself is demonstrated; for there is a contradiction between that which has not yet come into being and that which has already ceased to be—
namely, the blackness [of the jar] and the contact of the jar with fire, which has ceased once the color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*) has arisen in the jar.
The intention is that it has been stated that cause and effect are not the grounds for inference; this refers to what is accepted by the opponent.

Now, one might object: "In that case, while cause and effect characterized as 'the produced' and 'the producer' have been refuted there, those characterized as 'the manifested' and 'the manifester' have not.
This is not a fault.

For the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is indeed nothing other than the relationship between the produced (*janya*) and the producer (*janaka*). To explain: when auxiliary causes such as light are present, the manifestation of jars and the like is simply the production of another momentary state capable of generating cognition, which depends upon the material cause (*upādāna*); otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that the jar would produce cognition even without depending on the assistance provided by those [auxiliaries].
Others, however, maintain that for insentient things like jars, manifestation is a distinct property (*rūpa*) separate from their production.
And its own nature is not apprehended.

If it is argued that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is the capacity to produce cognition, then it follows that the jar and so forth themselves are produced by the manifesting agent; for that capacity is identical with their own nature. Alternatively, if it were a distinct entity, it would follow that the jar and so forth would not be assisted [by the manifesting agent].
Furthermore, since cognition arises from that capacity, it would follow that the jar and so forth could never be perceived.
For it is not logical that an object should exist without a cause.
If you argue that it possesses efficacy toward that [effect] even then, then it should produce it even when alone.
If you say it depends on auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*), [then...]
If it is argued that [the cause] produces [the manifestation] rather than [the object itself], what kind of dependence could there be for that which cannot be assisted?

If it is claimed that "manifestation" is simply cognition, then the consequence follows that jars and other objects would never be perceived, as they are eternal; thus, all these same objections recur.
Therefore, the manifestation postulated by others is not tenable.
Therefore, there is no relationship of sign and signified between them.
Nor is a composite substance such as a cloth perceived as something distinct from its constituent parts such as the threads;
therefore, since its existence is negated by the non-perception of its own nature, it does not exist at all.
How, then, can there be an inference of that [composite] by means of those [parts], or of those [parts] by means of that [composite]?
Even if that [reason] exists, it is not logical to infer from it because of deviation; this has already been stated.

It might be argued as follows: "The inference that an effect arises from a complete cause is incorrect, because perception is admitted to be of a determinate nature (*niścayātmaka*). For a cause must either be productive—being free from any possibility of obstruction—or non-productive due to the presence of an obstruction.
In the former case, since it is determined by that [determinate] perception in its specific form, there would be an inference of the production of a specific effect from that very [cause]."
And yet it does not exist.
For instance, when people act for the sake of an effect by discerning it from its cause, they are seen to be deceived.
But in the second case, once there is the certainty that "this is not even a cause," how could there be an inference of the possibility of an effect arising from it?

For when it is certain that fire is not the non-cause of cold, no one would infer the occurrence of cold from fire. Thus, according to the view of the opponent, cause and effect are not grounds for inference.
"Conjunction [is not a cause] because it is not established in the case of what has not yet arrived.
That which, even when unperceived, does not result in an inference regarding something else, is not the cause of that inference;
for example, fire with respect to water.
Furthermore, even when the conjunction of fire and smoke has not been apprehended, the inference of fire occurs;
this is [an example of] the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
But how is there proof when that [conjunction] is not perceived? He says: "For it is seen," and so forth.
Since conjunction resides in two things, its apprehension—like the number two—necessarily occurs only after perceiving all of its substrata.
And at the time of inference, because no substratum is perceived at all, the apprehension of conjunction is simply impossible.
Moreover, fire is inferred by means of smoke through the recollection of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*).

It might be argued that this cause of inference could exist even when it is not known; to this he says, "precisely as a cause of cognition," which means "as a cause of the cognition of its own object.
For every indicator makes known the object to be indicated only by producing a cognition of its own object, just like a lamp.
Otherwise, there would be cognition of fire even from smoke that has not been grasped [as such].
"And of conjunction," and so forth.
That which is the locus of a conjunction is the cause for the cognition [of its correlate] when there is a second counter-correlate;
for example, smoke.
And thus, he states a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by saying, "fire.
(78) It might be argued: "This is indeed accepted," to which he replies with the words beginning "and it is observed" (*dṛṣṭaś ca*).
But surely, even smoke is observed to exist in bedchambers and the like without fire?
What, then, is the distinction between these two cases, such that the consequence of being a manifestor is raised against one but not against the other?

The thought is as follows: although the smoke’s state of being in conjunction (*saṃyogitva*) does not exist in the present, it certainly did exist previously; for that which is caused by a specific occasion (*naimittika*) does not deviate from its cause.
At the very moment it arises, the smoke is conjoined with fire.
Fire, however, is merely the instrumental cause (nimitta) for that [perception]. And it is not necessarily the case that every instrumental cause possesses its corresponding effect.
Therefore, in a certain state, even its former state of being conjoined is no longer possible.
Thus it is: since fire is sometimes the cause of smoke and sometimes not its cause, it lacks definiteness (*vyabhicāritva*) and therefore cannot be the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of smoke.
However, if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) were intended as the cause of inference, then that [status of being a manifestor] would follow; this is what is being objected.
"From the refutation," and so forth.
He states that it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the doubtful scripture, since it is a cause for doubt.
But how is it that, while the state of being conjoined is equal, fire is inconclusive and smoke is not? To this he says: "For that [fire] is not necessarily... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "due to non-difference":
conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed attainment (*prāpti*);
and there is no difference in that [attainment].
And therefore, just as there is the attainment of one [fire], so too there is the attainment of the second;

it is not logical for there to be no cause for [the presence of] fire in a single location. This might be the case: there is some variable substratum of conjunction which deviates from that [conjunction].
There is something non-deviant which does not deviate;
therein, that alone which is its non-deviant substratum is intended as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and nothing else.
Therefore, the mere apprehension of the conjunction is not the cause of inference. What then?

When this [conjunction] is apprehended through prior investigation as having a substratum that is either deviant or non-deviant—specifically, as "this has a deviant substratum" and "this has a non-deviant substratum"—only then, upon a non-deviant substratum...
We accept that [the relation] possesses the capacity to convey [the meaning].
Therefore, since inference must be performed by means of that very non-deviant [relation], there is no room for the aforementioned fault; thus he says, "For not," and so forth.

Whether it is apprehended once or repeatedly, the conjunction (saṃyoga) does not acquire any excellence of its own nature (*ātmātiśaya*) by which it might become the cause of inferential cognition when it is apprehended repeatedly.

And if, even though it has already been apprehended, that [invariable concomitance] must still depend upon being apprehended as the basis for both the deviant and the non-deviant, then in that case, a relation of "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvitva*) entirely different from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would have to be admitted. Therefore, if that were accepted, its apprehension should be established by a single instance alone.
And therefore, how could there be an investigation into whether this [reason] is deviant or non-deviant?
To the question, "How is it that this fault does not also apply to one for whom the relation is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*)?", he says: "But for one [who holds]... and so forth.
