The inclusion of the word "necessarily" is because inseparable concomitance, such as between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), exists in both [the subject and the locus].
And by the passage beginning with "nor by anyone," etc.:
that form of fire which is conjoined with smoke is cognizable through smoke, just like the form of fire and so forth;
and such is the form of the blazing [fire] and so on.
Likewise, that which is the form of smoke (*dhūma*) as conjoined with fire is the indicator (*gamaka*) of fire, just like the form of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) and so forth.
And thus, he states two *svabhāvaprasaṅga* [reductio ad absurdum] arguments: "and likewise, it has the form of a substance (*dravya*), etc.

By the mention of "flaming" (*dīpta*) and so forth here, only the form of fire itself is expressed, and not the universal (*sāmānya*) of the quality (*guṇa*), because conjunction is impossible for those two.
"And as [stated] in the passage beginning with 'yathā ca'": this extends the aforementioned fault to other types of relations.
"But because [the property] is possible in the case of contradictories.

By the inclusion of the term "possible," he demonstrates that this *prasaṅga* (reductio) applies only when the contradictory is actually existent, and not when it is non-existent, because in the latter case, the distinction between the general and the particular would be untenable.
Regarding the passage beginning with "liṅgasya" (of the mark):

that which is the generality (*sāmānya*) of the mark—such as smoke and so forth—which consists of [the categories] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like, and those which are the particulars (*viśeṣa*), such as being ablaze and so on; both of these are not the indicator (*dyotaka*) and the indicated (*dyotya*).

And here, a mediated connection (*vyavahita-sambandha*) is to be understood: the generality and the particulars of the mark are not the indicator and the indicated of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
This has been stated thus for the sake of metrical conformity;

however, for others such as the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, it follows [absurdly] in every respect that the indicator and the indicated are identical, because the relation—such as conjunction and the like—is indistinguishable.
"The consequence of apprehending merely that which is conjoined" means that the object to be inferred would be grasped merely by way of its form as something conjoined.
Why is this so? He says: "Otherwise," and so forth.
For a logical mark (*liṅga*) makes known the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) in accordance with its relationship.

Therefore, a mark (*liṅga*) that causes cognition by virtue of its connection must, when apprehended in the form of one related thing (*saṃyogin*), cause cognition in that very same form, because the state of being related (*saṃyogitva*) depends upon another related thing.

Thus it has been said: "When this [mark] is well-known as being related to this [object] and is free from doubt, then, through the apprehension of this related thing, there arises a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) even with respect to the related thing that is not being perceived."
It might be argued as follows: conjunction occurs precisely through the form of fire;
therefore, there is also cognition [of the object] through that form.

As for what was stated previously—namely, "Now, of this... and so forth—in that context, by the term "related" (*sambandhinī*), a specific [relation] is intended, and not merely the nature of being a conjoined or inherent substrate. To this he says: "And not here... and so forth.
Alternatively, without raising a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another defect by means of this [passage]:

if the existence of fire were to be proven by means of smoke as its conjoined correlate (*saṃyogin*), then the conjunction of fire and smoke would constitute a constituent factor (*aṅga*) in the inference;
however, that [conjunction] is not what is being proven.
He asks, "Why? and says: "Because that [nature] is already established.
If so, then what is being proven? He says: "But where," and so forth.
Whence is this [known]?
From the statement "here" (atra). For by the word "here," the locus-ness of the place is established.

But surely, it is the commonality of the substratum that is established here by this statement. To the question, "In that case, how can there be an understanding of a specific [substratum] from that? he says: "For otherwise," and so forth.
By this, he indicates that the qualification excludes any other possible meaning that would be impossible.

Where there is a statement such as "the other meaning is impossible here," there is an intended reference to the location as the substratum (*pradeśādhāra*), as in the sentence "here in this well. And the statement "here" in the phrase "the fire is here" is likewise [an instance of this].
The task.
[The opponent objects: "But is the qualification not unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is intended by the phrase 'of smoke alone here'? To this he replies: "In smoke, fire," and so forth.

However, the charge that it is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*) arises because the very subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is stated as the reason (*hetu*). [The opponent continues: "But the particular (*viśeṣa*) is a part of the meaning of the proposition, while the universal (*sāmānya*) is the reason."
Whence, then, does this fault arise?

He thinks as follows: by one who desires a conjunction—that is, a connection—between fire and smoke, the cause must also be accepted as a particular (*viśeṣa*) consisting of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not a universal (*sāmānya*); otherwise, conjunction would be impossible.
For according to the treatise (*śāstra*), that [conjunction] is held to exist only between two substances (*dravya*).
Consequently, the reason becomes a part of the very meaning of the thesis.
In this case as well, it must certainly be stated: "And here the existence of fire is not being proven, because that is already established," and so forth.
Therefore, that [reason] alone should be called a rejoinder (*uttara*) where the aforementioned fault does not apply.
But here, even when a specific smoke is the reason and fire is the probandum, that same fault remains exactly as it was;
therefore, this is not a valid reply.

If, then, it is your established tenet that conjunction occurs only between two substances, then fire also must be accepted as a particular (*viśeṣa*)— a synonym for the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)— insofar as it is the probandum (*sādhya*). Consequently, since both the probandum and the probans would consist of unique particulars, every reason (*hetu*) would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of both the probandum and the probans.
This is true.
For this very reason, he says: "Therefore, there is no necessary conjunction between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin).
Here, the word "to be accepted" (abhyupeya) is to be supplied.

Since there is thus a fault in conjunction—that is, in a relation of contact—therefore, a relation of conjunction must certainly not be accepted between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*). By the use of the word "necessarily" (*avaśyam*), a restriction is indicated;
for what then?
It is precisely the state of being inseparable (*avinābhāvitva*), because that is free from fault.
But is not that [inference] also indeed faulty because it is non-pervasive?
For it does not exist at all times for the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Indeed, smoke is sometimes perceived even in places and times devoid of fire; thus he says: "But depending on place and time," and so forth.
Insofar as smoke has not been observed in a particular location without fire, it possesses "inseparability" (*avinābhāvitva*) with respect to that location.

Or, insofar as smoke has been perceived as inseparable from fire during a certain duration of time—such as during the state of rubbing fire-sticks together, or other states where fire is present—it possesses inseparability with respect to that duration; this also applies to "inherence" (*samavāya*) and so forth.

A relation that is not perceived cannot be a cause of inference, just as the causal relationship between two things is not established for someone to whom it is unknown. And since inherence (*samavāya*) is unestablished, [the author] states the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāva*).
The passage beginning with "For a relation... is an illustration of this point.
The phrase "for not," and so forth, is an elaboration of that very point.
Regarding the expression "even for one who is untrained":

it is observed that even for one who lacks linguistic proficiency regarding the category of inherence (*samavāya*), there occurs a correct cognition of a cow or similar object upon the recollection of its invariable concomitance with horns and the like.

Therefore, invariable concomitance alone is the cause of inference, because [the probandum] possesses that [probans] both when it exists and when it is absent, just as a seed [is the cause] of a sprout.

With the words "here too, this very same... and so forth, he states that inherence (samavāya) possesses the same defects as [the other categories]; and with the words "here too, moreover... and so forth, he also states that conjunction (saṃyoga) possesses the same defects. It might be argued: "The non-existent and the doubtful are non-indicators (anapadeśa)," and thus there is an exception; therefore, there is no inference of wind from color or touch. To this he replies: "And if there were deviation... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "from the cause of the cause":
the head is the cause of the body;
the forehead, which is its own part, is the cause of that [head] as well.
Furthermore, from that very cause of causes, a cognition [of inherence] is observed in the body, which is the effect of the effect.

But how can there be inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) between the body and its head-part, given that inherence in a single object has been shown to be of two kinds due to the difference in the nature of the composite (*vigraha*), namely: "inherence in a single object"? For instance, the head is one object.
And by that, there is a conjunction of both of them as well.
Regarding the phrase "as he said," he states that very statement as the proof.
For one for whom this is well-established and beyond doubt— that those [beings] beginning with the head do not arise without having commenced a body,
and that upon the destruction of this [body], the non-destruction of the body is impossible.
Furthermore, since the parts of the head and so forth do not become separated when [the head] has not been destroyed, one forms the cognition: "There was a body of which this is a part.
Therefore, it should not be determined that [the object of cognition] is only of two kinds.
But surely, the cognition arises from that very head which is seen and then destroyed, and not from its parts?
Therefore it has been said: "from what has not come into being. This is because that which is non-existent cannot function as a cause, just like an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*).
In order to refute the claim that contradiction (*virodha*) is a cause for inference, he says: "That which is contradictory," and so forth.
For the conjunction of wind and clouds is indeed contradictory to the action of raining, because the two cannot coexist.
Furthermore, the action of raining is not the logical mark (*liṅga*) here, because it establishes a property that is contrary to it.
What then? It is the absence of that; for when there is a conjunction of wind and cloud, the action of raining is absent.
Nor is there a contradiction between the absence of the action of raining and the conjunction of wind and cloud, because they coexist.
It might be argued: "The absence of the act of raining is itself a particular state of that very act;
therefore, the act of raining, having reached a certain state, is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
But how can an absence be a particular state of something existent?
Or, if it were a particularity (*viśeṣa*) of that [entity], then non-existence itself would not exist, because a particularity is of the nature of existence.
Or, if it were a different entity (*arthāntara*), the same fault applies: "that which is contradictory is not a logical mark (*liṅga*). This is no answer.
(86) The same should be stated elsewhere as well;
that is, wherever there is an inferential mark (*liṅga*) of something non-existent, it is also [to be understood] there.
For indeed, the absence of contact between wind and clouds is contradictory to the absence of the action of rain.
And here, the absence of the act of raining is not the indicative mark;
what then?
It is the act of raining itself.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the rain-activity and the conjunction of wind and clouds; the same applies to the case of "one element [producing] another element. Likewise, the activity of fluidity, namely flowing, is opposed by the construction of a dam.
And movement is not the probans;
what then?
It is its absence.
The same applies here to the case of "the non-existent [arising] from the non-existent.
There is a contradiction between blackness and contact with fire;
moreover, there is no relationship of indicator and indicated (liṅga-liṅgibhāva) between these two in this instance.
What then?
[It refers to] the cessation of those two.
And as for what was said:

Because of the statement in the treatise that "existence, non-eternality, possession of substance, being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity" constitute the common characteristics of substances, qualities, and actions, it is stated therein that only substances, qualities, and actions possess the nature of being causes. However, since the status of non-existence as a cause is asserted here by such statements as "the non-existent [is the cause] of the existent," the question arises: how can non-existence be an indicator (liṅga) of existence?
We do not say that non-existence is the mark of existence; what then? It is the cognition of "it was not" and so forth.
Why?
Because an instruction is preceded by what is already well-known (*prasiddha*).

Only for one person who has previously established the connection at the time of grasping the relation—that "smoke is conjoined with fire"—does there arise, upon seeing smoke, an inference regarding fire; not for anyone else.
Therefore, it is the cognition of smoke and so forth that is the inferential mark (liṅga);
however, the status of being an inferential mark attributed to its object is merely figurative, as in the expression "the sandalwood scale."
"Because there is no connection, there is no cognition of the mark (liṅga).
That which has no connection with something else cannot be its mark, just as a jar is not the mark of a cloth.
And since there is no connection between the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) and the cognition of the mark, [the author] states the absence of the pervader (vyāpakābhāva).
And regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing a connection":

when it was stated that "the self is indicated by its well-known [synonyms]," the opponent replied: "Well-known synonyms are not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the self, because they are distinct from it.
For one thing cannot lead to the cognition of another thing, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."
Therefore, this sūtra is presented.
This is what is meant: not everything is an indicative mark (liṅga) of something else;
rather, what is it?
That which is connected by any one of the relations, such as cause and effect and so forth, with [the subject] is precisely what constitutes an *apadeśa* (probans).
"Because it is designated as being inferential (laiṅgikatvena).

Since the word "inferential" (laiṅgika) is used in this sūtra, the cognition of the mark (liṅga-jñāna) is designated as being inferential; therefore, to claim that it [the cognition] is itself the mark (liṅga) would result in the contradiction of one's own accepted position.

Now, if you think that it is the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) that is indicated here as "inferential" (*laiṅgika*), and not the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), he says: "For in the cognition of the object to be inferred," and so forth.
If the cognition of the mark were intended to be the inferential [cognition], then the cognition of the object to be inferred would be its distinct result.

If, however, the cognition of the inferable object were itself the inferential result (*laiṅgika*), then since that object would already have been apprehended at the time of the arising of that [cognition], there would be no fruit [of the inference]. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with what has been accepted.
It might be argued: "The cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is the inferential means (*liṅga*), and the recollection of the connection is the inferential result (*laiṅgika*)."
"But the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is the result.
Therefore, he says: "It is merely a memory," and so forth.

If the recollection of the relation were itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even one who does not perceive the logical mark (*liṅga*) would have the cognition of fire from the mere recollection of the relation between smoke and fire.
The word *mātra* (only) is for the purpose of excluding the perception of smoke;

for it is precisely the recollection of the relation accompanied by that [perception] which is accepted as inference, as it has been said: "Both of these are inference because they are the causes of inferential cognition, either directly or through a succession."
Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of the particle *iti*": this refers to the reading of the particle *iti* at the end of the sūtra, namely, "and that which is contradictory.
The particle *iti* indicates that knowledge such as "this is the effect of that," and so forth.

If, then, inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika*) were [identical to] the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*), then even for one who is untrained, there would be comprehension from the mere perception of the mark.
Therefore, he says: "dependent upon the recollection of the relationship.
That it depends upon the recollection of the relationship is understood from the fact that an *apadeśa* (a formal statement) must be preceded by what is already well-known.
"Having made it the cause" (*kāraṇaṃ kṛtvā*):

this word *liṅga* is a synonym for "cause," because verbal roots have multiple meanings; its etymological derivation is "that by which something is marked (*liṅgyate*) or produced (*janyate*), namely the effect. [This constitutes] the cognition of the mark (*liṅgapratipatti*). (89)
And thus, it does not fail to be the cause for the cognition of the inferable object.

Therefore, as for what was stated— that because there is no connection, the cognition of the mark is not the mark— and that this [objection] is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) because the intended sense is that of a "cause-as-reason" (*kāraṇahetu*),
he refutes that with the words beginning "that is not so" (*tac ca na*).

"In the object of inference" (*anumeye*) means "of that which has become a mark" (*cihnabhūtasya*), which signifies "of the indicator" (*jñāpakasya*), because by this [mark] the object of inference is marked—that is, known.
"Otherwise" (*anyathā hi*) means:

if the status of being a logical reason (*liṅga*) were to apply even to that which is a producer (*janaka*), then the contact between the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects would also have to be mentioned [as reasons].
For those [other factors] are also causes for the cognition of the inferable object,
yet they have not been mentioned.
Therefore, that which merely produces [the cognition] has no standing here.

It might be argued: "The cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is the direct cause of the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), and nothing else; therefore, because it is the primary cause, only the cognition of the mark has been mentioned. To this he says: "And not directly," and so forth.
How is it not [the direct cause]? He says: "Because it is mediated by the recollection of the relationship (*sambandhasmṛti*)."
"The establishment of the recollection of the relationship would occur.
From this statement, the recollection of the relationship would be established, but not the cognition of the related object, such as smoke and so forth.
For thus says the Bhāṣya: "For whom the relationship of smoke and so forth with fire and so forth is established," and so on.
He provides a supporting indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this meaning, stating that it will be explained as follows:
because it is stated in that very same place—“How is it understood that an instruction (*apadeśa*) is necessarily preceded by what is already well-known? It is said:
because when there is the existence of another [unestablished] object, that which is not well-known is not an instruction.”

How so? For smoke and the like are not "indicators" (*anapadeśa*) for one to whom the relationship between smoke and fire, etc., is not well-known; therefore, this [example] does not prove that the cognition of the mark (*liṅga-jñāna*) is itself the object characterized by the mark (*laiṅgika*).
Regarding the statement "being an effect and so forth were not set forth in the Sūtra":

in the treatise, it was stated that "sound is non-eternal because of being an effect, because of its cause, because of modification, because of conjunction, because of disjunction, and because sound is produced from sound"—thus, being an effect and the other reasons for the non-eternality of sound were mentioned.
Likewise, for the sake of establishing eternality, it was stated that "that which exists and lacks a cause is eternal," thereby mentioning the state of existing without a cause.
Since the status of these [reasons], such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth, has not been stated as being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*), there is a deficiency in the definition.
To this, one might object: "But those [reasons] like being an effect are already included within [the categories of] effect and so on. To this he replies: "For not even one of these," and so forth.
The meaning is that not even a single one among these logical marks, such as impermanence (*anityatva*), [is mentioned].

Is it not the case that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and "being existent yet causeless" (*sadakāraṇatva*) are included within "inherence in a single object," since "being an effect" and "impermanence" inhere in a single object such as sound, while "permanence" and "being existent yet causeless" inhere in a single object such as the self? This is not so.
For it has been stated that an effect inherent in the same substrate as another thing can be the cause of another effect or another cause;
however, in this case, the relationship of cause and effect is not possible.

(91) Regarding the phrase "by way of the manifested and the manifestor": impermanence is an effect because it is that which is manifested; however, being an effect is a cause because it is that which manifests. This should be understood in the same way for other cases as well.
It follows that the remainder would be non-expressive;
otherwise, there would not even be a separate mention of it,
yet such a mention does exist.
Therefore, it is understood that in this context, the relationship of cause and effect is not intended by way of the manifested and the manifestor.
"That too is useless because [the object] is reached from another [source]" means that it is useless, i.e., devoid of purpose,
because [the object is already known] through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

For, by virtue of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), one understands from a mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke that which is to be inferred; it is then conceived by the mind that "this [mark] is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of this [object]. Therefore, the implication is that its status as a cause of inference is postulated in vain.

Alternatively, the word "conceives" (*kalpayati*), which is the subject under discussion here, should also be connected [to the previous sentence]: the opponent postulates its status as a cause of inference even though it serves no purpose. This is the meaning.
Others, however, say: "In this treatise, it is indicated that the relation which is the cause of inference is indeed inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
The mention of relations such as the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is, however, for the purpose of demonstrating the different types of inference.
Consequently, there is no fault whatsoever."

That is incorrect, because the cause is also indicated as a logical mark (*liṅga*), and since that [cause] exists through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), even inference based on possibility (*sambhavānumāna*) is not impossible according to the opponent's own view.
(93) "Also for the Sāṅkhyas," and so forth.

Since it has been established that inference exists in detail, the opponent asks—"What is this so-called inference?"—in order to fully understand its nature. To this, [the author] replies: "From one [of two related things], by means of the connection," and so forth.
"Connection is sevenfold.
Its sevenfold nature is established by the statement in the Bhāṣya, "of connected meanings, [the connection] is by way of the relationship between owner and owned," and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the designation "of connected meanings," it should be understood that in the Sūtra the word *sambandha* is used in the passive sense (*karmasādhana*).
"Or by way of the relationship of owner and owned," as in the case of a king and his servant, and as in the case of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa).
These two examples are given by virtue of their renown in common worldly experience and in the scriptures, respectively.
It should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
The relationship of owner and owned is mutual.
The state of the owned toward the owner is its fitness for that role;
likewise, the state of the owner toward the owned is the same.
Or [the relationship may be] by way of the state of being the material cause and its modification, as in the case of curd and milk, or as in the case of the Pradhāna and the Mahat, etc.
Nature (*prakṛti*) is the undivided cause;
modification (*vikāra*) is that of it. (94)
The nature [of transformation] is transformative (pāriṇāmika).

It occurs through the state of cause and effect, characterized by mutual assistance—like the parts of a chariot or like the qualities such as *sattva*—in the process of transformation into the form of sound and so forth;
or it occurs through the state of sign and signified, characterized by assistance from one side—like a potter and a jar, or like the functions of the Puruṣa and Pradhāna.

Either by way of the relationship between the whole and its parts, characterized as the relation between a part and that which possesses parts—like a tree and its branches, or like the great elements such as sound;
or by way of the relationship of companionship—like the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*) and its mate, or like the [three] constituents (*sattva*, etc.);
or by way of the relationship between the victim and the slayer—like the mongoose and the snake, or like the limb and the possessor of the limb, and so forth.
For whichever among the *sattva* and the other qualities possesses the status of being the dominant factor (*aṅgin*), it overpowers the others.
This is the sevenfold relationship.
Therefore, it is "from one [thing] through a connection as far as possible," as it has been said:
"A certain object becomes perceptible to a certain sense organ.

Consequently, from that object which is presently perceived by the sense organ, the cognition—based on the connection established previously with the aggregate—comprehends the existence of the undifferentiated object.
For example, having previously observed the connection between smoke and fire, one realizes the existence of fire upon seeing smoke.

(95) Regarding the phrase "the cause of establishment": the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), which depends upon the recollection of the relationship [between the mark and the object], is the cause for the establishment (*siddhi*) of that specific related object which is not perceived. Establishment, however, is the result.
In the Sūtra, however, it is stated that "the establishment of the remainder is inference" by means of applying the name of the effect to the cause.

However, the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅgajñāna*) may sometimes be indeterminate; for instance, in one who perceives mere paleness and so forth—which are common to both smoke and vapor—there arises doubt: "Is this smoke, or is it vapor and the like?
Furthermore, it is "incorrect" because there is the apprehension of vapor and such as being smoke.
Thus, he begins the subsequent [definition] for the sake of providing a qualification.

Regarding what was stated—"from a single perception"—this is its qualification: "perception that is not determined. It is "perception" because it is grasped through the general functioning of the auditory organ and so forth; it is "not determined" because it is not ascertained in its specific detail due to doubt and error.
"Because of the perception of a specific quality (*viśeṣadarśanāt*).

Those which distinguish [something] are "specific qualities" (*viśeṣāḥ*). From the perception of those specific qualities—such as whiteness and so forth—which exist only in smoke, one recognizes it specifically: "This is indeed smoke," and so on.

By the word "all," he indicates the remainder of the text. That [remainder] is as follows: (96) when, in a place suitable for cows or horses where the light is very dim, one sees a form the size of a cow and the intellect is in doubt, it arrives at a specific determination through the perception of particulars—namely, "it is a cow" or "it is a horse."
"Having seen the formless" means having seen slight form; that is to say, having seen mere shape.
"Thus, when it is desired [to be established]" (*evaṃ ceṣyamāṇe*) means when that which was previously apprehended in a general way is again apprehended in its particularity.

"Because it consists merely in the observation of its own object" (*svārthālocanamātratvāt*) means because it consists merely in the experience of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound and so forth.
The word "merely" (*mātra*) is intended to exclude the apprehension of universals and particulars.
"For it is not [the case] that the activity of the ear and so forth... and so on.
For the universal and the particular depend upon other objects;
therefore, by depending on another object, there arises the notion that "this has similarity with that" or "this is the particular of that."

Nor does the operation of the auditory and other senses possess such a capacity for apprehension, because it is non-conceptual; thus, neither the universal nor the particular is the object of sensory operation. This is because [sensory cognition] would not correspond to reality regarding its object, which is the universal. For it has been said: "Indeed, perception is both universal and undetermined."

That very [term] must be stated as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), such that "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the operation of the ear and other senses in accordance with their objects; this is according to the *Nyāyasūtra*. For when it is stated in this way, the definition of perception becomes faultless, and here there is no [need for a further] qualification. (97)

An action must be performed [only] when the mark has been ascertained; otherwise, because it would not be perceived, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it could not function as a mark at all.

On this point, some say: "Even if perception consists merely in the observation of its own object, it does not follow that it lacks the generality-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) as its domain; for sound and the like are not distinct from the general and the particular, and thus sound and the like are in every respect objects of the sense faculties. This is incorrect, because it would entail a contradiction regarding the determination of [perception's] own specific object.
The universal that exists in the operation of the word "sound" is the very same one that exists in "form" and so forth.

And just as that [universal] is non-different from sound, it is likewise non-different from form and the rest; thus, if it were apprehended through the operation of the auditory organ, it would follow that form and the rest are also apprehended.

Furthermore, because the universal is non-different from the manifold forms and so forth, the universal would possess multiplicity, and because the forms and so forth are non-different from that single [universal], they would possess unity.
"Direct perception has direct perception as its fruit.
As for what was stated—"one who desires it thus," and so forth—this is the rebuttal: because mental activity is conceptual and has both generalities and particulars as its objects.
That too is incorrect.
If the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) were to have direct perception as its fruit, then such a designation [of it as "perception"] would be appropriate;
however, that is not the case because their objects are distinct.
And this has already been stated previously.

Therefore, it is incorrect to designate [the object] by the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). He demonstrates this with the words "nor of anything else," and so forth; for there is no reason to metaphorically apply the designation of the object to anything other than perception itself or its fruit.

(98) Alternatively, some explain it thus: in the phrase "from one perception" (*pratyakṣāt*), the word *pratyakṣa* indicates well-known status (*prasiddhatva*). The meaning is "from a well-known perception.

By this, even for another cognition—whether it be a perception itself or the fruit of perception—there will be the designation "perception" with respect to its object, which is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, he says: "Nor [is it established] by another," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: for establishment must occur through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest.
Among these, it is first of all not tenable that it is established by direct perception, according to the method already described.
Nor can it be established by inference, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
For whatever mark (*liṅga*) is used to infer smoke, another mark must be sought to establish that [first] one;
and for the establishment of that [second] one as well, yet another is required—thus there is the consequence of an infinite regress.
Scripture (*āgama*) also does not always function toward the apprehension of gender;
for those who do not rely on the established tenets (*siddhānta*) and conventions (*samaya*) do not determine gender by means of scripture.
Furthermore, this [position] is incorrect because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "A certain object becomes perceptible to a certain sense organ."
"Let it be granted for the sake of argument that there is some way of designating this as 'perception'; nevertheless, wishing to state another fault, he says: 'And this must be stated,' and so forth.
The apprehension of the owner (*svāmin*) and so on must occur either in their form as 'ownership' (*svatva*) and the like, or in some other form.

If they are apprehended in the form of ownership and so on—such that [the object] is grasped simply as 'one's own' (*svam*)—then, since ownership belongs to the owner, ownership is impossible without an owner; therefore, because it necessarily depends upon an owner, [the cognition] would result from the observation of a gender-indicative mark (*liṅga*)."
One must first of all have the cognition of ownership;
for otherwise, there would be no such apprehension as "this is his property.

Consequently, the subsequent recollection of the relationship would be purposeless, because the ownership of the master would already be established, leaving no room for a remainder [to be proven], and it is accepted that the establishment of a remainder constitutes inference.
If, on the other hand, it is intended that the apprehension occurs through some other mode, then [that mode] has not been stated, and thus the definition is incomplete.
This applies equally to the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*).

For if the apprehension of the mark is by way of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*), and since this inseparable connection necessarily depends upon another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then the object to be proven (*sādhya*) must already have been cognized prior to the apprehension of the mark. And if that were so, regarding the object to be proven—
If the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is already established, the recollection of the relation is redundant.
Alternatively, if it were otherwise, then what was stated [previously] would not hold; thus the point is the same.
"Not of that," and so forth.

From the statement "presence in the object of inference" (*anumeye sadbhāva*), only the mere presence of smoke and so forth in the locus (*dharmin*) is grasped, not its state of being related [to the probandum].
To the question, "When then is that [relation] grasped?", he says: "Afterwards," and so on.
"By one who has not mastered it" means by one who is ignorant of relations such as that between property and owner; "by the understanding of the remainder" is the meaning.
But how is that [relationship] understood? He says: "For it is seen," and so forth.

Regarding the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), just as the relationship of cause and effect is analyzed in the treatise (*śāstra*), it is precisely that lack of proficiency [in understanding it] which is intended here, and not its total absence;
for in the treatise, the relationship of cause and effect is established through transformation (*pariṇāma*) while a single entity does not abandon its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, even those who do not comprehend the relationship of cause and effect in that manner determine the inferable [object] by means of another method, through the perception of mere inseparability (*avinābhāvitva*). However, the relationship of cause and effect as seen in the scriptures is simply untenable;
for if the effect and the cause were identical, it would not even be possible to say, "this is the effect" and "this is the cause."

Now, if there were some excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) belonging to those two by which such a consequence of difference would arise, for even in the case of existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities, the very basis for establishing their difference is indeed a difference in intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that, although there is a difference in terms of being cause and effect, there is oneness because of the non-difference of the genus (*jāti*) "the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*), [we reply: ...

Since the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) are not perceived apart from cause and effect, and since transformation—whether successive or simultaneous—is impossible for that which is eternal, how could there be a causal relationship based upon them? Enough of this digression.
It might be argued that it is precisely when unapprehended that it is the cause of inference; to this he says: "And not," etc., which is easy to understand.
And as for the phrase "not necessarily," etc.:
[an objection is raised]—"But surely the establishment of the nature of the 'own' (sva) depends precisely upon the 'owner' (svāmin);
so how can there be any deviation?"

He thinks as follows: either the mark (*liṅga*), grasped as belonging to oneself at the very time of inference, would cause one to cognize the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); or else, having been determined as such at the prior time of grasping the relation, it might be perceived otherwise at the time of inference. If it is maintained that at the time of inference it is the means of cognition when it is ascertained that "this is its own," then the fault already stated applies here—[as in verse 101]:
"Ownership [is established] from the relation with the owner," and so forth.
Therefore, one would have to accept a second perception; and from that, there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Since it is possible for the relationship between owner and owned to be reversed in turn, it is impossible to make such an inference: "This was previously apprehended by me as belonging to him."

Therefore, since it is possible to perceive things such as a parasol even when they are ownerless and exist independently of a king or other such master— on the grounds that "wherever this [parasol] exists, there its owner must also exist"—
one should infer a similar deviation (*vyabhicāra*) elsewhere as well, according to the circumstances.
It might be argued: not everything that is related through a relationship such as that of property and owner is an indicator;
rather, it is that which is non-deviant.

Therefore, he says: "For [it is not the case] for one who has apprehended the relation," and so forth. If, even when the aforementioned relation has been grasped, the mark (liṅga) were again observed to be both deviant and non-deviant, then only the state of being inseparable (avinābhāvitva) would be the cause of inference, and not relations such as that of owner and owned.
It might be argued: "Inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is the cause of inference; that [connection] exists when the aforementioned relation is present; therefore, that [relation] is specified."
That is incorrect, because even when that [cause] exists, this [effect] may be absent.
"Because the relationship is not distinct.
For the relationship between a cause (nimitta) and its effect (naimittika) resides in both [terms].
Since it exists in one place, it must likewise exist in the second; thus, the status of signifier (gamaka) and signified (gamya) would apply to both.
(102) The relationship between the slain and the slayer, however, is indeed no relationship at all; such is the intended meaning regarding the sign (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the sign (*liṅgin*).
For this very reason, he says: "For those two are not the sign and the bearer of the sign.
Other types of relationships are possible between the sign and the bearer of the sign according to the view of others.
Furthermore, the relationship of the slain and the slayer is not possible even according to the opponent's own view.

For instance, the relationship of the slain and the slayer exists between a snake and a mongoose; yet these two are not intended to be the "mark" (*liṅga*) and the "marked" (*liṅgin*), because there is a deviation [from that rule]. Rather, it is the victory of the snake and the defeat of the mongoose.
And between those two, there is no relationship of the slain and the slayer.
The same applies elsewhere as well, such as in the case of the crows and owls and so forth.

Furthermore, by the words "that which has been determined" and so forth, he states that [the definition] lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*), because inference— which is the cause for the realization of the conjunction between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*— is not included.

Regarding the phrase "by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes limited magnitude (*parimāṇa*), the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), capacity (*śakti*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and heterogeneity (*vaiśvarūpya*).

In the phrase "the realization of giving, existence, and so forth," the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the supplementary topics such as non-duality, purposefulness, and being for another's sake.
Then, [the author] asks "which one? because not even one among the seven is possible.
[The answer is] "it must be considered," because two possibilities exist.
It need not be stated separately;
one should say, "Pradhāna exists because differences are observed," rather than "because the persistence of differences is observed."
For the specific manifestations (bhedas) alone are "conditioned" (naimittika), because they are produced;
the "condition" (nimitta) is the Pradhāna, because it is the producer.

(103) "Because of non-difference": the universal (*anvaya*) is also the very essence of the particulars (*bheda*), since it is their property (*dharma*); and because the property and the substratum (*dharmin*) are non-different, it is therefore logical that this [universal] is likewise adventitious (*naimittika*), just like the particulars.
In this same way, it should be understood for measure and the other [characteristics] as well.
It is not fivefold;
because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the others are of the nature of difference, the *vīta* would be merely a single type, namely difference itself.

And by the words "na ca kaścit" and so forth: those primary attributes (*pradhānadharmas*) which bring about the various manifestations (*bhedas*) are understood through them, just as [the nature of] unity and so forth [is understood].
Likewise, [attributes such as] being partless and formless are [understood].

Similarly, those derivative attributes (*bhedadharmas*) which are brought about by the primary cause (*pradhāna*) are indicators (*gamakas*) of that [cause], just as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth [indicate it].
And likewise, he states two consequences regarding intrinsic nature: "the mastery over sentient beings" and so forth.

Now, even if the relationship between cause and effect exists in every respect, there is no consequence of [the sign and the signified] being related as indicator and indicated in all respects, because such certainty does not exist. For indeed, according to statements such as "one perceives an object that is both perceptually present and undetermined in its particulars through the observation of its particulars," the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is accepted as being of the nature of a certainty; and since the properties of the mark intended to be uncertain are not distinct from that [certainty], this [objection] is not a valid answer.
(104) This might be argued: "Indeed, such a relationship between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) is accepted. To this he says, "Of the differences," and so forth.

Since in the treatise it is precisely positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the rest that are grasped as the logical reasons (*hetu*), and not mere existence (*sanmātra*) and so forth; and since it is precisely the existence of the *pradhāna* and the like that is to be proven (*sādhya*), and not its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and so forth—therefore, this relationship of cause and effect (*nimittanaimittikabhāva*) is not the means for understanding the existence of the *pradhāna* and other such principles.
But how can the Pradhāna be partless, given that existence (*sattva*) and the other qualities are indeed its parts?
There is no fault here, for it is "partless" because there are no parts distinct from those [three qualities].
Thus, there are ten summarized topics (*cūlikārtha*).
Existence, unity, purposefulness, subservience to another, distinctness, lack of agency,
conjunction, disjunction, the plurality of spirits, and the persistence of the body through residual activity.
Thus these are to be understood. Therefore, that which is appropriate here is what is fit; and that is indeed inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva).

[Objection: But surely that [the relationship between cause and effect] is already implied by the state of being the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*), because the effect is invariably concomitant with its cause. [Reply: True, it is implied; however, by the opponent... (105)

One who maintains that a logical mark (*liṅga*) connected by the relation of essential identity (*tādātmya*) is the indicator must also admit that a cause (*nimitta*) is an indicator, because that too is connected with its effect.
Since the relationship of indicator and indicated exists in every respect through the relationship of cause and effect, this undesirable consequence follows for him:

if, on the other hand, one were to accept that whatever possesses an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) by way of the cause-and-effect relationship is the indicator, then the cause-and-effect relationship would not exist in every respect, and thus nothing undesirable would follow.

With the words "tathā" (likewise) and so forth, he extends the aforementioned fault to other types of relations as well. "By a part alone" means by some particular aspect. "The state of being unrelated has been explained" [refers to what was stated previously].

The term "lack of relation" (*asambandhatva*) should be understood as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Its meaning is that it denotes a type of relatedness other than the relatedness belonging to a relation that serves as the cause for the cognition of the object to be inferred.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction, because it would be impossible for relations to possess a lack of relatedness.

But surely, relations such as that between owner and owned are illuminators; therefore, by means of them, the inferential mark (liṅga), while illuminating [the object], illuminates it only through some particular aspect because it conforms to its own relation. Why, then, is there a relationship of signifier and signified in every respect? To this he says: "Merely by way of being owner and owned," and so forth.
From its own perception, there would be a cognition of the king and so forth solely in the form of "being a master," and not in specific forms such as Śrīharṣa and the like.
Why? He says: "Otherwise, in the case of cognition," and so on.
If the capacity for apprehension were admitted to exist apart from conformity with its own relation, then that alone would constitute the relationship of signifier and signified in every respect.
(106) "Even by a portion of ownership," and so forth.
For a portion of ownership is connected merely with the state of being an owner.
Therefore, if—on account of conformity to that connection—it is maintained that it reveals only that [owner] itself, then the mere state of being an owner would cause the possessor to be known.
He asks "Why? and says "For not," etc.; the meaning is that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the communication [of a word] if it were independent of its relation [to its object].
"In the transgression of that" means in the transgression of the matter just mentioned;
that is to say, if the capacity to communicate its own object existed in some other manner apart from the door of its own relation, rather than in accordance with its own relation.
"Enough with this digression," he says,
showing that the relationship between property and owner and so forth— namely, the sign and the bearer of the sign— were introduced merely as a digression.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor":
if the relationship between cause and effect is intended to be the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor,
then one should not state that the manifestor is solely the relationship between cause and effect.
He asks "Why? and says: "It is sevenfold."
For the relationship between the signified and the signifier is indeed the relationship between the manifested and the manifester.
Furthermore, since that which is to be inferred is understood through all seven types of relations,
it must be admitted that [the manifestation] itself is likewise sevenfold.
Otherwise, other things would lack the capacity to manifest [it],
because they are different from it— meaning they are distinct due to the relationship between cause and effect.
(107) "As was stated previously" means that this very point was already expressed by the statement, "That too is useless, since [the object] is understood from something else."
Furthermore, one should not say that there is a relationship between the sign (*nimitta*) and the signified (*naimittika*).
If both the sign and the signified were indicators (*gamaka*), it would indeed be appropriate to speak in such a way.
However, neither both are indicators; rather, it is only the signified that is the indicator.
He demonstrates this: "Because here, being a cause (*nimittatva*) is what constitutes manifestation.
For in this context of the conventional usage of inference and the object of inference, being a cause is precisely what manifests [the relationship].
But what, then, is this so-called "being a cause"?
The "sign" (nimitta) refers to the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) of smoke and other such signs with their respective probanda.
That by which the word "sign" is applied there is its "state of being a sign" (nimittatva).
This is not "being caused by a sign" (naimittikatva); rather, it is connected with the term "manifestor" (vyañjaka).

In this case as well, that part of the probandum which is to be understood constitutes its being a "contingent" (naimittika) factor. Why, then, is being contingent not a manifestor? He says: "Because it is what is to be manifested" (*vyaṅgyatvāt*), which means "because it is the probandum" (*sādhyatvāt*).
For only that which is already established (*siddha*) can be a manifestor, not that which is yet to be established (*sādhya*).
Therefore, one should simply say "the state of being a cause," and not "the state of being cause and effect."
It might be argued as follows: it is not understood that "the state of being between the cause (nimitta) and the effect (naimittika) is the 'state of being cause and effect'.
For if it were understood in that way, the mention of the "effect" would be redundant, since the state of being the cause alone would suffice to indicate it.
How, then, is it to be understood? It is as "the existence of the cause by means of the effect."

Furthermore, that inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is the cause for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, considering it both the "cause" (*nimitta*) and the "cognition" (*pratyaya*), if only the term "causal state" (*nimittabhāva*) were used, it would not be known with what the causal state characterized by inseparable relation exists.
Therefore, the employment of a derivative term is for the purpose of apprehending the counter-correlative.

This is not so; for since a cause (nimitta) necessarily depends upon its effect (naimittika), even if it were stated in this way, there would still be a cognition of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin). Thus, the mention of the "effect" is fruitless.
As for what was said [previously], he extends that same refutation to another philosophical system (darśana).

The state of being concomitants (sahacaribhāva), however, is the non-existence of [properties such as] positive concomitance and so forth in the absence of a primary [subject]. And it is not merely the state of being concomitants;
rather, through positive concomitance and the other [criteria], there is the comprehension of primary objects that are beyond the senses.
Furthermore, it is stated in the treatise that inference *śeṣavat* is the means for the comprehension of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*).

However, this [inference] is not applicable as *śeṣavat* when the relationship is one of coexistence (*sahacaribhāva*), because of the primary connection with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.
For coexistence is not the same as the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), since they are mentioned separately.
Furthermore, concomitance exists only between two things that are established as co-existent, like the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*).
However, there is no simultaneity between cause and effect, because at the time of the effect, the cause has already disappeared. Therefore, how could there be concomitance from that? (109)
The apprehension of supersensuous objects through inference and other means is accepted [by you].
That [apprehension] is not tenable if the relationship is merely one of concomitance; thus, your own position is abandoned.

Therefore, it is not only this [reason] that must be accepted; another must also be sought, since through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, the existence of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and other principles is established.
Inference is of two kinds.

Among these, *viśeṣadṛṣṭa* (inference based on perceived particulars) is when, having observed the connection between fire and smoke, one repeatedly ascertains the existence of that very same fire by means of that very same smoke, thinking, "This is that very fire.

*Sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is when, having observed the connection between smoke and fire in some instance, one subsequently infers the general category of fire from the mere sight of smoke.

This inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam anumānam*) is also of two kinds: that which has a prior [effect] (*pūrvavat*) and that which has a remainder [or subsequent cause] (*śeṣavat*).
Among these, *pūrvavat* is when, having observed a complete cause, one understands the future existence of the effect;
for example, having seen the rising of clouds, one understands the future existence of rain.
The *śeṣavat* [inference] occurs when, having observed the completion of an effect, one realizes the existence of its cause;
for example, having seen a river with newly increased waters, one realizes the existence of a cloud.
Among these, the inference based on what has preceded (*pūrvavat*) is fallible, whereas the *śeṣavat* is free from error provided it is accompanied by careful deliberation (*savicāra*).
Among these, that inference which is based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*), namely the *śeṣavat* type, is the means for the apprehension of entities that transcend the senses.
(110) He states the justification for the claim that "recollection is [a means of valid cognition] along with [perception]" in the passage beginning with "for not...

By this, he states the essential nature [of recollection]: that which identifies "this is that very same thing previously experienced" is of the nature of recollection, such as the cognition "this is that very same smoke. And he states its intrinsic nature by saying that "the particular-observation" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) possesses the aforementioned characteristics.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of effect and cause" (*kāryakāraṇābhyām*): the purpose of the restriction that "the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* alone is of two kinds" is indeed the exclusion of any other twofold division.

Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that there could be no repeated inference by means of effect and cause; for if one were to maintain that repeated inference constitutes *viśeṣadṛṣṭa*, it would result in the abandonment of one's own accepted position (*abhyupetahāni*).

With the words "Now, [if it is argued]... and so forth, he states the very abandonment of what has been accepted; for the result of the restriction that "sāmānyatodṛṣṭa is of only two kinds" is the exclusion of any other number.
Consequently, by means of relations such as owner and owned, there is first of all no inference [of the self].
The inclusion of the term "first of all" is because, in the case of repeated inference, the possibility of *viśeṣatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on specific observation) exists.
Why is there an absence of the *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* [inference]? He says: "For in these cases, there is no relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

And it is from the relation of cause and effect that the *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* is intended. Why is there an absence of the *viśeṣadṛṣṭa*? He says: "Because there is no apprehension of a particular (*viśeṣa*)."

In the second and subsequent moments, the apprehension of a distinction is possible—namely, "this is that very same thing"—which is called the apprehension of its continued existence; this occurs because of the apprehension of a distinction, but not in the first moment.
The relations are specified as being of seven kinds, such as the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) and so forth.
Inference is said to be "only of two kinds" because it is possible for other types to exist besides those based on general observation (*sāmānyadṛṣṭa*) and specific observation (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*).
The first word *tu* has the sense of "because," while the second has the sense of "therefore."

Since inference is indeed of only two kinds, where then could the three types of inference—consisting of the master and so forth—be placed when it comes to the initial apprehension of the object to be inferred? The point is that they have no inclusion within those two at all.

The mention of "three" is because the categories of cause and effect, modification and its substrate, sign and its indicator, and measure and what is measured, are all included within the very relationship of cause and effect.
"Because of the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor" means because of the relationship between the one who receives assistance and the one who provides it.
For the relationship of owner and owned is not possible without the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle (atiprasaṅga).

By this same method, the relationship of cause and effect is inferred for both the relationship of association (*sahacaribhāva*) and the relationship of the victim and the slayer (*vadhyavadhakasambandha*); thus, they are not mentioned separately.
For instance, there is no association without mutual benefit, as is seen in the case of the two *cakravāka* birds, who provide mutual assistance through the sharing of sexual pleasure and so forth.

Furthermore, the relationship of victim and slayer—such as between the victory of a snake and the defeat of a mongoose—is indeed a relationship of cause and effect, because they serve as causes for one another, just as the qualities of *sattva* and the others undergo transformation into the form of sound and the rest.
"Because it would follow that there is no other relation.
There would be only the single relation of cause and effect, and no other relation;
for there is no relation without the state of being the beneficiary and the benefactor. (112)
This is not possible, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
How, then, is there an absence of any other relation? To this he says: "In all cases," and so forth.

When an inference is to be performed by means of all seven types of relations, an assistance—either mutual or belonging to one or the other of the two related terms, as the case may be—is already provided by those two related terms, namely the signified (*pratyāyya*) and the signifier (*pratyāyaka*).
Otherwise, there would be no connection between the two at all.
Alternatively, *anumāna* is that by which something is inferred; it is the sevenfold relationship. In that *anumāna*, the locative case has the sense of "occasion" (*nimitta*).
The sevenfold relationship is the cause (*nimitta*). The remainder, beginning with "by the signified and the signifier," is as before.
In this interpretation, there is this objection: "But surely the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is relied upon for the purpose of signification?"
Otherwise, there would be inference even from a mark whose relationship is unknown upon its first observation.
Therefore, how can it be said that "this alone is the assistance"? For there is no occasion for such an objection, since "assistance" is not intended here as the act of making something known.
What then?
Favor is that which constitutes the very self of the two related parties.

"The fault is twofold" means that this very [fault] pertains to both positions. "The absence of a result" is because the results of sentences consist in the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntaravyavaccheda*).
With the words "For what [would there be] for this," etc., he demonstrates that very absence of a result.
Now, one might object: surely the result of the sentence would simply be the demonstration of the two-fold nature [of the object], which has not yet been understood;
why then is it necessary here to exclude other meanings?
This is incorrect.
For its own nature is cognized through the exclusion of other objects, because it consists in a form that is differentiated from other intrinsic natures.
If another form were not excluded, how could there be a cognition of its own nature?
Furthermore, this twofold nature is not unknown, as it has been introduced in the context of inference based on cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇānumāna*).
In that regard, the repetition [of the term] is understood to serve the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
To show why that [interpretation] is incorrect, he states the reason: "because the related [term] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*)."
Regarding the phrase "the possibility of obstruction and so forth":

obstruction (*pratibandha*) refers to the occurrence of a counteracting condition (*vidhurapratyaya*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the possibility of a deficiency in auxiliary causes (*sahakārivaikalya*) is included.
"It is indicated" (*liṅgyate*) means "it is understood. A figurative usage (*upacāra*) is not appropriate here, because there is no basis for such a figurative application.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha":

for one who, having seen a certain cause produce an effect and seeing another thing of the same kind, has a mind led astray by similarity, determines that "this too will certainly produce that effect."
From that [cause], knowledge of the effect arises;
however, because of the statement "sometimes," it does not arise at other times.
Since it does arise, it is called inference (anumāna) because it has the nature of being the cause of inference.
Because it does not occur at all times, it is called "erroneous" (*vyabhicārin*).
Thus, both its nature as inference and its erroneous character have been explained.
Therefore, at that time, because it is not a cause for that [cognition],
even then the metaphorical designation of "inference" is not tenable, since it lacks the status of being a cause of inference.
For that which is an unreal cognition is certainly not inference itself at that time.
Therefore, it is not logical to apply the metaphor of "inference" to its cause.
Furthermore, when it is in accordance with reality, there is an absence of deviation;
thus, there exists nothing that could be both a single instance of inference and yet deviant.

But surely, even that which causes a fallacy of inference is called "invalid" (*amāna*). For instance, speakers say: "The inference put forward by him has been refuted by me," or "It is inconclusive" (*vyabhicārī*).
Since this much is intended to be expressed, he says "yadi ca" and so forth, [arguing] that this is not a valid refutation.

If, even when there is knowledge of the causal relation, one further requires a degree of deviation or non-deviation that has arrived as another relation, then you are abandoning your own established position.
The phrase "of which alone non-deviation is required" means "of which alone the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of non-deviation is required.
Why is it called the "essential nature"?
Because for that which possesses inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*), there is no other non-deviation, since that [inseparable connection] itself is the very form of non-deviation.
By the words "In all inferences," etc., he states the pointlessness of the repetition.
If that statement is for the sake of restriction, even so, there would be the pointlessness of the passage beginning with "Indeed, even in a general way."
"And this deliberation concerns the existence [of the mark].
Here, the word *sattva* (existence) denotes the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

For when the relationship between cause and effect is accepted as the basis for inference, it is appropriate to deliberate upon the very nature of the mark (*liṅga*) itself—namely, whether "is this an effect or not?"
For example, [the case of] "a river in flood" (nadīpūra).
For in that instance, the investigation concerns the very nature of the object itself: "Is this river in flood caused by rain, or is it not?
But once its nature has been ascertained through such signs as being turbid with foam and muddy water, one no longer requires an investigation into its non-deviation [from the cause].
For once it is ascertained that [the cloud] has rain as its effect, no suspicion of deviation from that [effect] is raised, because an effect does not deviate from its cause.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Even though it is unexamined," and so forth.
Therefore, the restriction [that inference is the sole means] is not tenable, because there is the apprehension of supersensible objects through other means as well.

But is it not the case that the restriction is not formulated thus—"only inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is the cause for perceiving supersensible objects"? How then is it formulated? It is formulated as: "inference based on general observation is indeed the cause for the perception of supersensible objects.
And in this way, since there is no denial that other forms of inference can be causes for the comprehension of supersensible objects, there is no fault.
This is not the case;

for since all forms of inference are causes for the apprehension of what is imperceptible, it follows that *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* inference also serves as a cause for such apprehension. Therefore, when it is mentioned again, it is understood as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) consisting of the exclusion of its opposite, just as in the statement, "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten."
And from among the two types of inference, *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is distinguished and adopted as the cause for the comprehension of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*).
From that [inference] as well, it is understood to belong to that very [object].
For example: "The black cow has the most abundant milk"—thus, the state of having the most abundant milk belongs to the black cow alone.
"Because its very existence is the cause" means because the existence of the Pradhāna itself [is the cause].
For the Pradhāna is the cause of differentiation by virtue of its mere being, not by such attributes as oneness and so forth.
He thinks thus: "Of that which is non-existent... (116)
The addition [of new qualities] is denied in the case of modifications—namely, that this manifest world does not arise from what is non-existent.
Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), the various distinctions arise solely from the existence of the Pradhāna.
Furthermore, because the distinctions conform to the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), the cause must be of the very nature of existence itself.
And its self-sustaining nature as *sat* (being) is indeed intrinsic;
it is not produced by a connection with a universal *sattā*, because such a *sattā* is impossible prior to transformation.
Thus he says: "It is neither being nor non-being."

Just as existence does not exist at that time, so too do oneness and the other [qualities]. How, then, could they possess causality? Furthermore, the activity of the primary cause (pradhāna) proceeds solely for the sake of diverting the longing of the spirit (puruṣa).
Therefore, causality belongs to that very [consciousness] alone.
If this is so, how is it that it was stated: "And there is no differentiator whatsoever of the Pradhāna, nor [is there any other cause]," and so forth?
That was stated precisely from the perspective of the opponent's own view.

If the opponent, having accepted non-difference, were to establish the ten points of the *Cūlikā* concerning the purposes of the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, then in every respect the goal would be achieved.
This, however, is according to our own intention—namely, on the grounds that it is logical that only the actual existence of that [cause] constitutes its causality.
And its existence as the primary [cause] is established precisely from those very particulars.
By the words "of the existence of the sentient being" (*sattvasya bahutvasya vā*) and so forth, he explains the meaning of the word *sarvathā* (in every way).
From the word *vā* (or), the sense of conjunction is understood, as in "of oneness" (*ekatvādeḥ*).

"Either by distinction or by non-distinction" means either by [the property of] existence (*sattvena*), or by [the property of] oneness (*vaikena*), or by [properties such as] being without an agent (*akartṛkatvādibhiḥ*); or else, by one [reason], or by five [reasons]; or again, whether existence and so forth are distinct from the person (*puruṣāt*) or even non-distinct.
To claim that there is no understanding whatsoever would entail the abandonment of your own accepted position.
Whatever is not a cause cannot be determined by inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*), just like absolute non-existence;
and such is the case with the Puruṣa.
This is the absence of pervasion (*vyāpakābhāva*).

However, those who—asserting that when a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) arises which reflects the activity of the sense organ transformed into the form of sound, a corresponding modification also arises in the person (*puruṣa*), and therefore the person undergoes transformation into the form of that modification—bring forward the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*); for them, the person would consequently become of the same nature as primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
For instance, the mental modification consists of the three *guṇas*,
and the modification of the *puruṣa* takes on that same form;
consequently, the *puruṣa* itself would also consist of the three *guṇas*.
And thus, because the modification and that which possesses the modification are non-different, it follows that the person (puruṣa) also consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
And because he would possess the nature of the three qualities, he too would be nothing other than the primal matter (pradhāna); and in that case, the aforementioned fault applies.
Furthermore, the admitted oneness of the Pradhāna would be lost; therefore, this [objection] is without substance.
(118) "Inference and so forth," etc.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), verbal testimony, comparison, and presumptive testimony are included.
[The phrase] "because it is preceded by perception, it is just like that" means that inference and the others are likewise dependent upon perception.
Just as direct perception is without a sign (animitta) with respect to the Dharma, so too are inference and the other means of knowledge.
Why? Because they are preceded by direct perception.
For this very reason, these [other means of knowledge] were not set forth as aphorisms.
For what purpose would perception and the other means of knowledge be examined?
It is in order to make known that Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), and is not characterized by perception and the like.

And since it has been made known that perception is not a cause with respect to *dharma*, it is already understood that whatever else is preceded by perception likewise cannot be a cause for the thorough knowledge of *dharma*; so what is the point of stating that [in the Sūtra]?
How, then, are the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) recognized in the Mīmāṃsā? To this he says: "By the authors of the Vṛtti," and so forth.
With the words "In that regard," etc., he states the refutation.
Now, in the Sūtra, being preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakatva*) was presented as the reason for its not being formulated [as a definition of inference].

But in the Vṛtti, regarding the full comprehension of its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), it is stated: "If that which is preceded by perception is to be recognized as a means of valid cognition"—how then does the Vṛtti follow the meaning of the Sūtra?

In the Sūtra, the state of being preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakatva*) is presented as the cause of the non-composition [of the treatise] through a traditional lineage (*pāramparyeṇa*), not directly. And it is precisely to demonstrate that very lineage that the commentary beginning with "if that which is preceded by perception... was composed; thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, if [the question is raised regarding] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)... (119)

If "immediate" were said to mean that cognition itself is the cause of the non-specification [of the object], then the cause for the thorough knowledge of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not have been stated.
Consequently, there would be no room for the objection that memory, desire, aversion, effort, and so forth would follow as being [themselves] means of valid cognition.
Therefore, in order to provide an opening for this objection, it was stated: "because it is preceded by perception" (*pratyakṣapūrvakatvāt*).

Is it not the case that in the *Mīmāṃsā* it was not stated that these [means of knowledge] possess validity because they are preceded by perception, but rather that their status as non-causes with respect to *dharma* was explained? As he said: "And because they are preceded by perception, inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are also not causes [for knowing *dharma*].
Upavarṣa also stated that they were not mentioned [as means of knowing *dharma*] precisely because they are well-known [to be such].

For there is no such fault [in our position], since the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), such as direct perception and the rest, are well-known. However, it has been made known that they lack established status in this context— by the statement "and many are in disagreement"— nor has their definition been stated, by virtue of which their essential nature could be determined.
Furthermore, because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception, it is indeed understood that they are not valid means of knowing *dharma*.

Therefore, the commentators (*vṛttikāra*), while elucidating the intention of the author of the *Vākya* (Jaimini), state: "That which is preceded by perception is indeed recognized as a valid means of knowledge; therefore, [inference and the rest] were not mentioned.
It is possible that this too was an intended meaning inferred [by the commentators].
Otherwise, the previous intention would not hold.

For it is impossible to understand that other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not causes with respect to *dharma* without first knowing their own nature; thus, they ought to have been stated for the sake of fully understanding their nature.
Yet, they have not been stated.
Therefore, it is certainly the case that whatever is preceded by perception is indeed recognized as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
