Consequently, one might suspect that the commentators (*vṛttikāras*) have also inferred this to be the intention of the author of the *Vākya* [the *Brahmasūtra*] when they state that [other means of knowledge] were not mentioned.
And consequently, it would follow that even memory and the like possess the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they too are preceded by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "inference, instruction, and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), comparison (upamāna) and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) are included.
Instruction (upadeśa) is of two kinds: human (pauruṣeya) and non-human (apauruṣeya).
In this context, the former [type of inference] is what is being considered;
however, the other [type] is not even intended by others to be preceded by perception.

It has been stated that [perception] has an uncommon object (*asādhāraṇaviṣaya*). This uncommon nature of sensory cognition was established in the passage beginning with "of the dharmin which possesses multiple forms.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "and the relation has multiple substrata," the commonality of the relation is demonstrated; thus, that which is common is not the object of perception, just like a universal (*sāmānya*).
And thus, he points out the contradiction with the pervader (vyāpaka-viruddha) in the claim that there is a relation.
Furthermore, the demonstration that a universal (sāmānya) is not observed is made by the passage beginning with "Even if the universal...
No lack of pervasion (avyāpti) should be suspected here.
For sensory cognition is held to have a real entity (*vastu*) as its object;
and a unique entity is not common [to others],
whereas a relation is common.
Therefore, it is not a real entity;
consequently, it is not the object of sensory cognitions,
nor [the object] of those related to it, and so forth.

If related entities are apprehended as having the nature of a relation— by way of being conjoined (*saṃyogin*), inherent (*samavāyin*), and so forth— then they become auxiliaries for inference and the like; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), those that assist comparison (*upamāna*) and other means of knowledge are included.

Otherwise, even one who first perceives smoke without having learned its relation to fire—because it is not connected with fire—would infer fire from that smoke. Yet they do not perceive them in such a way; for since being related depends upon a relation, and since both the relation and the state of being related are imperceptible, it is impossible for those [objects] to be grasped by perception in their form as related entities, because sensory cognition consists merely in the observation of the object and lacks the capacity for synthesis.
"Due to the distinction between *dṛṣṭa-sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* and so forth":

*Dṛṣṭa* is that where the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) has been perceived. *Sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* is that where, from the observation of a relationship in some instance, there is the comprehension of a supersensible object (*atīndriyārtha*) by way of its general form (*sāmānyākāreṇa*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the categories such as *pūrvavat* and so forth mentioned by the Naiyāyikas are included.

With the words "In that regard," etc., he demonstrates that even according to the opponent's own doctrine, inference—which has those [categories] and their possessors (*tadvat*), such as inherence and its substrata, as its objects—is not preceded by perception, since inherence, its substrata, and the like are admitted to be imperceptible in the form of inherence, its substrata, and so on.
Thus, he shows that for inference, which is the locus of those [categories], there is no requirement of being preceded by perception.

Regarding the phrase "according to his view" (*tanmatena tu*): the mention of "his view" is because, according to his own position, both the conjunction and the conjoined objects are themselves imperceptible.
Regarding the phrase "having accepted that": [it means] having provisionally accepted that.
That opinion is connected with the word "that" (tat).
"And [it is] not the cause of inference.
The word "and" (ca) should be understood as displaced in its order and having the sense of emphasis; the meaning is that it is *not at all* the cause.
(122) "Because there is no distinction between the two," and so forth.
The conjunction is undifferentiated for both related entities.
Consequently, there would be a relationship of signifier and signified for both fire and smoke, because they are conjoined in every respect and in their entirety.
Nor are the two conjoined [objects] to be apprehended by way of their own nature;
for "own nature" refers to that form, such as smoke and so forth, which is perceived even by one who does not know the relationship [between them].
Therefore, they are not worthy of being attained.
He asks "Why? and says: "For [it is] not in inference," and so forth.
[An objection is raised: "In that case, there will be an assistance [to the senses] once those two have been apprehended in the form of being related. To this he says: "Nor... and so forth.

By the statement, "The conjunction is not the object of sensory cognition, nor is that which is conjoined with it," it is stated that there is no perception of the two conjoined things in the form of being conjoined (*saṃyogirūpeṇa*).

It might be argued: "Granted that inference and the other means of knowledge do not necessarily have perception as their precursor; however, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) intended for them is faultless, since no refutation of it is being stated. To this he replies with the words, "Inference, verbal testimony, comparison," and so forth. But how is it that [the definition] has not been stated according to his own intention? He says: "Because no other relation has been specified."

Indeed, no relation other than those accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others has been specified. Furthermore, as for this inference which Śabara has stated according to his own view—"Inference is the cognition of one part, not in contact with the senses, [arising] from the perception of one part for one who knows the relation"—that is of two kinds: that based on a relation perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha), (123)

And as for "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), if those same relations are intended, then that too is simply Vaiśeṣika inference. If, however, they are different, then since their specific nature has not been specified, it would be an unspecified form of inference.
Furthermore, memory also arises from the perception of one part regarding another part previously apprehended; thus, that too would be inference.
It has already been stated that the relationship itself is not apprehended by the senses;
therefore, it is incorrect to say that there is "perception of a perceived relationship" (pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandhatā) for that [inference].
But as for presumption (*arthāpatti*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), a negation is stated [of them], because they are established according to their own intended meaning.
"Taken for the purpose of placing [the vessel] on the fire and so forth, such as the pot":
by the first word "and so forth" (ādi), specific implements such as the grinding stone and the ladle are included; by the second, specific operations such as the pouring of water are included.
Their being "taken for the purpose" is due to the fact that cooking arises from them.
For without them, the completion of the cooking does not occur;
therefore, by the principle of "otherwise being impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*), all of that is indeed grasped as an implied meaning (*arthagṛhīta*).

But how can this be an inference, given that inference is said to be the perception of an object from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics? To this he says: "It is understood from the very mark of 'he cooks' (*pacati*)."
For the cooking itself is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the pot and so forth, because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with them.
This invariable concomitance, however, arises from the fact that [the cooking] originates from them.
Therefore, because it is produced from an inferential mark, it does not differ from inference, just like the inference of fire from smoke.

(124) Others, however, maintain that the cognition of cause and effect through presence and absence is *arthāpatti* (presumption), while others consider that very same process to be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called *yukti* (reasoning).
For example: when the eye exists, visual consciousness arises; when it does not exist, it does not arise.
Therefore, the eye alone is its cause.
Indeed, this inference is not tenable because of the absence of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For an example is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
yet, in this case, there is no establishment of an example by any other means of valid cognition.
For instance—even regarding this example of the seed and sprout that is accepted [by you], the causal relationship therein is established by this very same [argument].
Nor is it logical that the example should be established by the very same means as the probandum; for that would entail the fallacy of an infinite regress of illustrations.
Furthermore, that [example] is not itself a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For here the relationship of cause and effect is not being established, because there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans;
indeed, there is no causal relationship other than existence and non-existence,
and it is not logical for something to be established by means of itself.

Therefore, in this case, for the sake of one who is deluded, practical activity is established through the recollection of the subject's connection with its past state—just as paternity is established by the perception of a son—by means of the perception of the object.
For this very object is of the same nature as that in which you have elsewhere engaged in the practical usage of cause and effect;
therefore, let that usage be applied here as well.
And since a formal example is possible when the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is to be established, this is indeed an inference.

The formal application (*prayoga*) is as follows: wherever there is the state of "arising upon the existence of that" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*), there the conventional usage of cause and effect must be applied;
just as, for example, where the causal relationship has previously been established in the case of the seed and the sprout.
And the fact that visual consciousness exists only when that [eye] exists is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

(125) But Śabara says: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact because a seen or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for; for example, when Devadatta is alive, his absence from the house leads to the postulation of his being outside, which was not previously perceived.

Here, following the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), since that which is understood from verbal testimony is separately designated by the word "heard" (*śruta*), the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) refers to what is apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For example, "he lives" is an illustration of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by non-apprehension (*abhāva*).

The meaning is that Devadatta’s non-perception in the house—while he is alive—is apprehended through the means of knowledge of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), and this is not logically possible without his existence outside [the house].

In this regard, if it is said that the non-perception of the living Devadatta in the house does not occur otherwise than through his being outside—that is, it is not possible otherwise—then even though he is invariably concomitant with being outside, he is not seen; thus, it still would not be possible.

Alternatively, if it is stated that the non-perception of the living Devadatta in the house is observed only when he is outside, and is not observed in his absence, such that it is not possible otherwise, then what is called "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) is simply the fact of its occurring only when that [other state] exists.
It may be so;

and since that [cognition] occurs only with respect to an object characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not differ from inference (*anumāna*). The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: he who meets the conditions for perception is not seen in the house, yet he is alive; therefore, he must be outside.
The nature [of the reason] is as follows: Yajñadatta, who is perceived externally in the manner previously described;
and Devadatta, whose existence is understood through the word and who possesses the properties previously described. This is the essential nature [of the reason].
(126) "Because it is a cause of doubt":

that which is a cause of doubt is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). And since the presumption (*arthāpatti*) under discussion is likewise [a cause of doubt], he states a reason that contradicts the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*).
"Because Caitra is not in the house," and so forth.
For the existence of Caitra outside is not cognized merely by his absence from the house; otherwise, it would follow for even a hare's horn.
However, the word "house" employed in that sentence makes known his existence outside.
For when the word "house" (*geha*) is employed, this sentence conveys a restricted absence, because such a sentence is used only when there is an intention to express that specific meaning.
As it has been said: "But if [the person] were not in the house nor outside, one would simply say 'he does not exist'.

Therefore, this sentence implies both the absence from the house and the presence outside, because for that which expresses the restriction of one [locus], the implication of the second is inseparable.
However, non-existence (*abhāva*) alone does not imply external existence (*bahirbhāva*), nor does a restriction (*niyama*) alone; for a restriction possesses a dual nature.
Therefore, when it is said, "Caitra is not in the house," it is not merely non-existence that is expressed, but rather his existence outside.
Consequently, non-existence is itself a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For just as the accomplishment of cooking does not occur without a pot and so forth, and thus the pot implies [the cooking] because of its invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*), so too, when there is an intention to express a restriction regarding negation, the use of the word "house" does not occur without being outside; therefore, due to that invariable concomitance, it implies being outside.

Consequently, just as the verb "cooks" is an indicator (*liṅga*) of the pot and so forth, in exactly the same way, the word "house" inherent in such a sentence is also an indicator of being outside; it is from that very word that the cognition of it arises.

(127) Śabara, however, says: "Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is the absence of [the other] five means of valid cognition, such as perception, regarding an object that is not in contact [with the senses], [expressed as] 'it does not exist. The absence of the five means of valid cognition, such as perception, serves as the cause for the ascertainment of non-existence regarding an object not in contact with the sense organ.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that non-existence is a means of valid cognition."

Others, who maintain that this is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), designate it by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) and say: "When an object is known through a certain apprehension, the non-existence of that [object] is known from the absence of that [apprehension];
this is considered non-apprehension."
Thus,
even in this case, the non-apprehension of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) cannot be the cause for apprehending the absence of an object if it is itself not apprehended.
If, on the other hand, it depends upon apprehension and functions toward the apprehension of the object's absence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For just as the absence of a jar is apprehended through the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too the absence of a means of valid cognition would be apprehended by another, and that by yet another; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*). Furthermore, if even one [instance] is not apprehended, then all are unapprehended—so how could it possess validity?

If it is argued that it might be a cause of apprehension like a sense faculty even when itself unapprehended, we say no; for the characteristic of non-existence (*abhāva*) is the absence of all causal capacity.

(128) Otherwise, it would be an existent entity (*bhāva*) itself, because existence is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*); therefore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"In that case, even for you, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), due to the very same fault [you have cited]. This is not so. For I do not accept non-apprehension in such a manner; rather, it is the non-apprehension of that which has met the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). The "conditions for apprehension" consist in the completeness of all other causal factors for apprehension (*upalambhapratyayāntarasākalya*) and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). That nature is such that, when the other causal factors for apprehension are present, if it exists, it is necessarily perceived.

In this context, apprehension (*upalabdhi*) would be either an action residing in the agent or an action residing in the object. In the former case, apprehension is the knowledge that is the property of the one who apprehends. Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is an apprehension other than that; because it is something other than the intended apprehension, it is like [the concepts of] "that which is not to be eaten" or "that which is not to be touched."

But when "perception" (*upalabdhi*) is used in the sense of an action residing in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*), then perception is simply a property (*dharma*) of that which is being perceived, characterized by its fitness for generating a cognition of itself;
this is because fitness is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).
Therefore, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is something other than that [perception], namely, that which is fit for perception and whose nature is conjoined with the same cognition as it.
Moreover, since this two-fold non-apprehension as it has been described is established by perception itself, the aforementioned fault does not apply to us.
(129) Let it be granted that such non-apprehension is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But how is it an inference (*anumāna*)? And why should it not be so?
Because it does not depend on examples;
for there is no example whatsoever in this [ultimate truth],
since an example must be established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, if the example were established solely through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), then just as the absence of a jar is established by means of an example, so too would the example— such as a "sky-flower" or other such non-entities—
be established by another example, and that one by yet another; thus, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would ensue.
Furthermore, if an example were established even without another example, then the absence of a jar would also be established;
consequently, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) would itself be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it does not depend upon an example.
This is not a fault;
for non-existence is not established by non-apprehension.
What then?
The linguistic usage of "non-existence" [is established as follows]:
for the basis (*nimitta*) of the linguistic usage of what is non-existent is the non-apprehension of that which is apprehensible.
Since this [non-apprehension], by its own presence, establishes this very basis of its own, everything here is an example of that which arises from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of its own basis.

Even when the probandum is the negation of the conventional usage of "existent," both sprouts and the like—which do not lack their causal conditions—are examples by means of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) and its opposite, and not merely the indefinable (*nirupākhya*); thus, there is no consequence of [this being] a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But what is the reason that non-existence itself is not established?
Because there is no difference [between them].
For it is thus: the very perception of things possessing a perceptible nature is their existence, and non-perception is their non-existence.
How so?

First, when apprehension is understood as the capacity to produce a cognition of its own object as previously described, then since this capacity is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the object, it is established that apprehension is existence itself.

Furthermore, even when apprehension is understood as the cognition that is the attribute of the subject (*kartṛdharma*), it is nonetheless not distinct from the nature of that [object], because it is dependent upon the existence of the perceptible object; for, through pervasion (*vyāpti*) and non-deviation (*avyatireka*), it is metaphorically designated as "existence" just like the existence [of the object] itself.
Existence alone is what it is. Thus, in both ways, existence is apprehension; and its absence is non-existence by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), as previously described.

And since that very non-apprehension is itself [the reason], there is no distinction between the probandum and the means of proof. Therefore, it is not the case that absence is proven by non-apprehension;

rather, by pointing out the cause, the conventional designation of non-existence is established through non-apprehension for the sake of a deluded person—just as one is designated a "father" through the act of procreation.

Even by means of non-apprehension through imperceptibility, there is a negation of conventional usage due to the absence of a causal sign (nimitta), just as [there is] the state of not being a father for one who has never fathered a son.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by the refutation of the opponent's position," etc.:

that which was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that the establishment of one's own position occurs through the refutation of the opponent's position—should be understood as having been refuted precisely by the refutation of the Sāṅkhya’s *āvīta* [type of inference]. This is because this [inference] is also indeed an application of the *āvīta*.
The second chapter is completed. (131)
